name: {\bf Density of Random Periodic Points}

title: Remark
body_md: The study of hyperbolic dynamics  goes back to Poinc\'are \cite{Poincare} on $3$-body problem and Hadamard \cite{Hadamard} on geodesic flow. The modern theory of uniformly hyperbolic dynamical systems was initiated by Anosov \cite{Anosov} and Smale \cite{Smale} where Anosov and Axiom A diffeomeophism/flows were introduced respectively. The core ingredient in these systems is the uniform hyperbolicity which is an invariant geometric structure describing the exponential divergence of nearby orbits. This exponential divergence together with the compactness of phase space produces rich and complicated dynamical structures. The dynamics of these systems has been understood very well. One of results is that for a transitive Anosov diffeomorphism, the set of its periodic points (the number of the periodic orbits with same period is finite) is countable and dense in $M$. However, Theorem A tells that for the systems we study here, the set of random periodic points  is uncountable because of the non-separability of $L^\infty(\Omega, M)$,  where we exclude the case that $\Omega$ has trivial topology. In fact, Theorem A indicates that  the cardinality of random periodic orbits with sufficient large period is infinite (actually uncountable), thus the increasing rate of numbers of random periodic orbits with same period as periods tends to infinity is always infinite. Therefore such an increasing rate fails in representing the topological entropy of the system, which is one of the main tasks that periodic orbits perform for Anosov diffeomorphisms in deterministic scenario. Nevertheless, there are other candidates which are able to carry out the task of representing complexity of the system such as the random horseshoes, which will be introduced in the next.

title: Theorem
body_md: {\it Assume that $\phi$ is  Anosov and topological mixing on fibers. Then the set of all periodic $\phi$-invariant measures is dense in $\mathcal I_{\mathbb P}(M\times\Omega)$ in the narrow topology. }
head: manual
name: {\bf Density of Random Periodic Invariant Measures}

label: E:PeriodicNull
title: Theorem
body_md:
{\it Assume that $\phi$ is  Anosov and topological mixing on fibers.
 Then for any $\Phi\in L^1_{\mathbb P}(\Omega,C^{0,\alpha}(M))$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{E:PeriodicNull}               
\int_{M\times\Omega}\Phi d\mu=0\; \text{ for any random periodic } \phi\text{-invariant measure $\mu$ with marginal } \mathbb P,
\end{equation}
there exists a functional $\tilde\Psi:L^\infty(\Omega, M)\to \mathbb R$ which is $\alpha$-H\"older continuous and satisfies the following cohomological equation
\begin{equation}\label{E:CoBoundary}             
\tilde\Phi(g)=\tilde\Psi(\tilde\phi(g))-\tilde \Psi(g),\ \forall g\in L^\infty(\Omega, M).
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\tilde \Psi$ is uniquely determined up to a constant functional.
}
head: manual
name: {\bf Random Liv\v sic Theorem}

title: Remark
body_md:
The celebrated theorem of Liv\v sic  \cite{Liv71, Liv72a,Liv72b} was established by  Liv\v sic for hyperbolic diffeomorphisms. Since then, there is a large amount of literature on generalizations of this theorem, see, for example, \cite{AKL18,dlLW10,dlLW11,Kal11,KK96, KP16,NP13,NT95, NT96, Wil13}.
Kifer and Liu \cite{KifLiu} conjectured that for a random Anosov diffeomorphism $f_\omega$ on $\mathbb{T}^d$, and a given function $\Phi(x,\omega)$ which is  measurable in $(x,\omega)$  and $\alpha$-H\"older continuous  in $x$, and satisfies $\int \Phi d\mu=0$ for any $\phi$-invariant measure $\mu$ with marginal  $\mathbb P$, the following cohomological equation
\[
\Phi=\Psi \circ \phi - \Psi+h,
\]
has a solution $(\Psi(x, \omega), h(\omega))$,  where $\Psi(x, \omega)$ is  a measurable function satisfying the random
H\"older condition $|\Psi(x, \omega)-\Psi(y,\omega)|\leq  K_{\Psi}(\omega)(d(x, y))^\alpha$ with  $\int \log  K_{\Psi}(\omega) \;d {\mathbb P}< \infty$, and $h(\omega)$ is a random variable with $\int h \;d {\mathbb P}=0$.

label: D:Anosov
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D:Anosov}         
The system generated by $\phi$ (or simply $\phi$) is called  {\bf Anosov on fibers} if the following holds:
for every $(x,\omega) \in M\times \Omega$ there is a splitting of the tangential fiber of $M_\omega:=M\times\{\omega\}$ at $x$
\[
T_xM_\omega=E_{(x,\omega)}^u \oplus E_{(x,\omega)}^{s}
\]
which depends continuously on $(x,\omega) \in M\times \Omega$ with $\dim E_{(x,\omega)}^u,\dim E_{(x,\omega)}^s >0$ and satisfies that
\[
Df_{\omega}(x) E_{(x,\omega)}^u=E_{\phi(x,\omega)}^u, \ \ \ Df_{\omega}(x) E_{(x,\omega)}^{s}= E_{\phi(x,\omega)}^{s},
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{E:UniformHyperbolic}                    
\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
|Df_{\omega}(x) \xi| \geq e^{\lambda_0} |\xi|, \ \ \ &\forall\ \xi \in  E_{(x,\omega)}^u, \\
|Df_{\omega}(x)\eta| \leq  e^{-\lambda_0}|\eta|, \ \ \ &\forall\ \eta \in  E_{(x,\omega)}^{s},
\end{array}
\right.
\end{equation}
where $\lambda_0>0$ is a constant.
head: environment

label: R:ContInvDistr
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R:ContInvDistr}               
It is clear that the splitting $T_xM_\omega=E_{(x,\omega)}^u \oplus E_{(x,\omega)}^{s}$ is uniformly continuous on $M\times\Omega$. Actually, one has that the above splitting is H\"older continuous on $x$, which follows from the standard arguments. Moreover, the H\"older constant and exponent can be chosen independent  on $(x,\omega)$. For more details, we refer the readers to \cite{Brin}, Section 5.3 of \cite{BaPe}, and Section  5.4 of \cite{LLL}.

label: D:Mixing
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D:Mixing}         
$\phi:M\times \Omega\to M\times \Omega$ is called  {\bf topological mixing on fibers} if for any nonempty open sets $U,V\subset M$, there exists $N>0$ such that for any $n\ge N$ and $\omega\in \Omega$
$$\phi^n(U \times \{\omega\})\bigcap V\times \{\theta^n\omega\}\neq \emptyset.$$
head: environment

label: D:RandomPeriodic
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D:RandomPeriodic}                 
$\{graph(g_i)|\ g_i\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)\}_{1\le i\le n}$ is called  a {\em random periodic orbit} of $\phi$ with period $n$ if
 for all $1\le i\le n$ $$\phi(\text{graph}(g_i))=\text{graph}(g_{i+1\mod n})\ \forall 1\le i\le n,$$
 equivalently,
 \begin{equation}\label{E:PeriodicPointTPh}                   
 g_i \text{ is a periodic point of }\tilde \phi\text{ i.e. }\tilde \phi (g_i)=g_{i+1\mod n}\ \forall 1\le i\le n.
 \end{equation}
head: environment

label: R:RandomDynSys
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R:RandomDynSys}               
The system generated by $\phi$ is usually called a skew-product system rather than a random dynamical system, which makes the name " random periodic orbit" sound a little bit more in name than reality. Nevertheless, once a $\theta$-invariant measure $\mathbb P$ on $\Omega$ is introduced,  the resulting system induced by $\phi$ becomes a random dynamical systems over the  metric dynamical system $(\Omega,\mathbb P,\theta)$ (see \cite{A} for more details).  On the other hand, since the name "random periodic orbit" has been introduced in exiting literature (see \cite{Kl, ZhZh}) and has the essentially equivalent meaning,  we prefer not to introduce different name or notions.

label: D:Horseshoe
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D:Horseshoe}            
 We  call a continuous embedding $\Psi:\mathcal S_k\to L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ a {\bf \em  horseshoe} with $k$-symbols of $\tilde \phi$ if
the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
     \item[i)] There exists $\Delta>0$ such that for any $l\in\mathbb Z$ and $\hat a_1,\hat a_2\in \mathcal S_k\text{ with }\hat a_1(l)\neq \hat a_2(l)$,
     \begin{equation}\label{E:SeparationImgSymbols}                       
     d^{\tilde \phi}_{l}\left(\Psi({\hat a_1}),\Psi({\hat a_2})\right)>\Delta,
     \end{equation}
     where for $l\ge 0$
     $$d^{\tilde \phi}_{l}(g_1,g_2):=\max_{0\le i\le l}\left\{d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}\left(\tilde \phi^i(g_1),\tilde \phi^i(g_2)\right)\right\},\ g_1,g_2\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$$ is the Bowen metric induced by $\tilde \phi$ and for $l<0$ we let $d^{\tilde\phi}_{l}=d^{\tilde\phi^{-1}}_{|l|};$
\item[ii)]  For all $\hat a\in\mathcal S_k$ $$\tilde \phi\left(\Psi({\hat a})\right)=\Psi({\sigma \hat a}).$$
\end{itemize}
head: environment

label: D:RandomHorseshoe
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D:RandomHorseshoe}                  
 We  call a continuous embedding $\Psi:\mathcal S_k\to L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ a {\bf \em  full random horseshoe} with $k$-symbols of $\phi$ if
the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
     \item[i)] There exists $\Delta>0$ such that for any $l\in\mathbb Z$ and $\hat a_1,\hat a_2\in \mathcal S_k\text{ with }\hat a_1(l)\neq \hat a_2(l)$
     \begin{equation}\label{E:RandomSepaImgSymb}                    
     \overline d^{\tilde \phi}_{l}\left(\Psi({\hat a_1}),\Psi({\hat a_2})\right)>\Delta,
     \end{equation}
     where for $l\ge 0$
     $$\overline d^{\tilde \phi}_{l}(g_1,g_2):=\max_{0\le i\le l}\left\{\overline d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}\left(\tilde \phi^i(g_1),\tilde \phi^i(g_2)\right)\right\},\ g_1,g_2\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$$  and for $l<0$ we let $\overline d^{\tilde\phi}_{l}=\overline d^{\tilde\phi^{-1}}_{|l|};$
\item[ii)]  For all $\hat a\in\mathcal S_k$ $$\tilde \phi\left(\Psi({\hat a})\right)=\Psi({\sigma \hat a}).$$
\end{itemize}
head: environment

label: D:SRandomHorseshoe
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D:SRandomHorseshoe}                   
 We  call a continuous embedding $\Psi:\mathcal S_k\to L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ a {\bf \em  strong full random horseshoe} with $k$-symbols of $\phi$ if
the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
     \item[i)] There exists $\Delta>0$ such that for any $l\in\mathbb Z$ and $\hat a_1,\hat a_2\in \mathcal S_k\text{ with }\hat a_1(l)\neq \hat a_2(l)$
     \begin{equation}\label{E:SRandomSepaImgSymb}                     
     \underline d^{\tilde \phi}_{l}\left(\Psi({\hat a_1}),\Psi({\hat a_2})\right)>\Delta,
     \end{equation}
     where for $l\ge 0$
     $$\underline d^{\tilde \phi}_{l}(g_1,g_2):=\max_{0\le i\le l}\left\{\underline d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}\left(\tilde \phi^i(g_1),\tilde \phi^i(g_2)\right)\right\},\ g_1,g_2\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$$  and for $l<0$ we let $\underline d^{\tilde\phi}_{l}=\underline d^{\tilde\phi^{-1}}_{|l|};$
\item[ii)]  For all $\hat a\in\mathcal S_k$ $$\tilde \phi\left(\Psi({\hat a})\right)=\Psi({\sigma \hat a}).$$
\end{itemize}
head: environment

label: R:CompareHorseshoes
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R:CompareHorseshoes}                    
Clearly, we have that
$d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}\ge\overline d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}\ge\underline d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}.$ Therefore, we have that  a strong full random horseshoe is automatically a full random horseshoe, and a full random horseshoe of $\phi$ automatically induces a horseshoe of $\tilde \phi$.

\label{R:WellDefined}              
First, one needs to show that the above integration is well defined and is finite. Since $\Phi(x,\omega)$ is continuous on $x$ and Borel measurable on $\omega$, we have that $\Phi$ is Borel measurable on $M\times\Omega$.  Then, for any real number  $a\in \mathbb R$,
$U:=\Phi^{-1}\left((-\infty,a)\right)$ is a Borel subset of $M\times \Omega$.
Note that $graph(g)$ is also a Borel subset of $M\times \Omega$ since $g:\Omega\to M$ is Borel. Therefore, $U\cap graph(g)$ is Borel in $M\times\Omega$. By applying Theorem \ref{T:BMST}, we have that $$\left\{\omega|\ \Phi(g(\omega),\omega)<a\right\}= \pi_\Omega\left(U\cap graph(g)\right)\text{ is Borel in }\Omega.$$
Hence $\Phi(g(\cdot),\cdot):\Omega\to \mathbb R$ is Borel measurable. As $\Phi$ satisfying (\ref{E:L1Holder}), we have that (\ref{E:Phi(g)}) is well defined and is finite.

label: L:LocCoor
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:LocCoor}          
For any $\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_0)$ there is a $\delta\in (0,\epsilon)$ such that  for any $x,y\in M$ with $d_M(x,y)<\delta$,  $W^s_\epsilon(x,\omega)\bigcap W^u_\epsilon(y,\omega)$ consists of a single point, which is denoted by $[x,y]_\omega$. Furthermore
$$[\cdot,\cdot]_{\cdot}:\{(x,y,\omega)\in M\times M\times \Omega|\ d_M(x,y)<\delta\}\to M\text{ is continuous}.$$
We say the system $(M\times \Omega,\phi)$ has {\bf local product structure} with size $\delta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: This simply follows from  iii) of Lemma \ref{L:InvMani}, the continuous (thus uniformly continuous) dependence of $W^s_\epsilon(x,\omega),W^u_\epsilon(x,\omega)$ on $(x,\omega)$, and the uniform continuity of the invariant splitting $E^u_{(x,\omega)}\oplus E^s_{(x,\omega)}$. For details, we refer to \cite{Bow4}.

label: L:Expansive
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:Expansive}            
There is an $\epsilon>0$ such that for any $\omega\in\Omega$ and $x,y\in M_\omega$ with $y\neq x$, the following holds:
$$d_M(\pi_M\phi^k(x,\omega),\pi_M\phi^k(y,\omega))>\epsilon\text{ for some }k\in\mathbb Z.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Take $\epsilon$ smaller than $\epsilon_0$ as in Lemma \ref{L:InvMani}. Otherwise, $(y,\omega)\in W^s_\epsilon(x,\omega)\cap W^u_\epsilon(x,\omega)$, therefore $y=x$.

label: L:Shadowing
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:Shadowing}            
For any $\beta>0$, there exists an $\alpha>0$ such that for any $(\omega,\alpha)$-pseudo orbit $\{(x_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$, there is a true orbit $\{(y_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$ of $\phi$ such that
$$\sup_{i\in \mathbb Z}d_M(y_i,x_i)<\beta.$$
$\{(y_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$ is called {\bf $(\omega,\beta)$-shadowing} orbit of $\{(x_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$.\\
 Further more, there is a $\beta_0>0$ such that for any $0<\beta<\beta_0$, the above true orbit is unique.

label: L:ClosingLemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:ClosingLemma}               
There exist $\alpha_0>0$ and $C\ge 1$ so that for any $\alpha\in (0,\alpha_0)$ and any $(\omega,\alpha)$-pseudo orbit $\{(x_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$, there exists a true orbit $\{(y_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ of $\phi$ satisfying the following
$$\sup_{i\in \mathbb Z} d_M(y_i,x_i)<C\alpha.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By i) and iii) of Lemma \ref{L:InvMani}, for any $\epsilon_1>0$, there exist $\delta_1, L_1>0$ such that the following properties hold
\begin{itemize}
\item[P1)] For any $x,y\in M$ with $d_M(x,y)<\delta_1$,  $[x,y]_\omega=W^s_{\epsilon}(x,\omega)\cap W^u_{\epsilon}(y,\omega)$ is well defined, where $\epsilon$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:InvMani};

\item[P2)] For any $x,y\in M$ with $d_M(x,y)<\delta_1$
$$\max\left\{d_M([x,y]_\omega,x),d_M([x,y]_\omega,y)\right\}\le L_1d_M(x,y);$$

\item[P3)] For any $x,y\in M$ with $d_M(x,y)<\delta_1$
$$\max\left\{\left|d_M([x,y]_\omega,x)-d_M([y,x]_\omega,y)\right|,\ \left|d_M([y,x]_\omega,x)-d_M([x,y]_\omega,y)\right|\right\}\le \epsilon_1d_M(x,y).$$
\end{itemize}
It is obvious that P1) holds when taking $\delta_1<\delta$ where $\delta$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:LocCoor}.
The proof of the  existence of such $\delta_1$ and $L_1$ to fit P2) and P3) may be standard, nevertheless, we  sketch the proof briefly for the sake of completeness. Note that  the above properties only appear in a local scenario, for the sake of simplicity,  we  fix an atlas of the manifold and always keep our discussion in one single local chart in the rest of the proof. Without causing any confusion, we identify $T_xM_\omega$ and $T_yM_\omega$ to $\mathbb R^n$ for $d_M(x,y)$ small, thus such $x$ and $y$ are considered to be two points in $\mathbb R^n$ thus $x-y$ are well defined, and $\exp{(E^u_{(x,\omega)})},\ \exp{(E^s_{(x,\omega)})}$ are considered to be  hyperplanes in $\mathbb R^n$, which contain the point $x\in \mathbb R^n$. We also note that the distance in the local chart $\mathbb R^n$ is equivalent to the metric $d_M$ and the comparison constant is some system constant, therefore we will not distinguish  them in the local argument.\\

Now we propose the condition of $\delta_1$ and $L_1$ which make P2) valid. As discussed in Remark \ref{R:ContInvDistr}, the splitting $T_xM_\omega=E^u_{(x,\omega)}\oplus E^s_{(x,\omega)}$ is uniformly continuous on $(x,\omega)$, thus one can make $E^u_{(x,\omega)}\oplus E^s_{(x,\omega)}$ closed enough to $E^u_{(y,\omega)}\oplus E^s_{(y,\omega)}$ by taking $d_M(x,y)$ small enough. Precisely, consider the splittings
$$\mathbb R^n=E^u_{(x,\omega)}\oplus E^s_{(y,\omega)},\text{ with associated projections } \pi^u_{x,y}, \pi^s_{x,y},$$
and
$$\mathbb R^n=E^u_{(y,\omega)}\oplus E^s_{(x,\omega)},\text{ with associated projections } \pi^u_{y,x}, \pi^s_{y,x},$$
then we request that for any $d_M(x,y)<\delta_1$, the following hold
\begin{equation}\label{E:ErrProj}          
\max\left\{\|\pi^\tau_{x,y}-\pi^\tau_{(z,\omega)}\|,\|\pi^\tau_{y,x}-\pi^\tau_{(z,\omega)}\||\right\}<\epsilon',  \tau=u,s,\ z=x,y,
\end{equation}
where $\epsilon'>0$ is a prefixed small constant.

Let $z_1=[x,y]_\omega$ and $z_2=\exp(E^u_{(y,\omega)})\cap \exp(E^s_{(x,\omega)})$. Note that, locally, $z_1-z_2$, $\pi^s_{y,x}(z_1-z_2)$ and $\pi^u_{y,x}(z_1-z_2)$ are well defined and satisfy the following:
$$d_M\left(z_1,\exp(E^u_{(y,\omega)})\right)\ge\frac{|\pi^s_{y,x}(z_1-z_2)|}{\|\pi^s_{y,x}\|} \ge\frac{|\pi^s_{y,x}(z_1-z_2)|}{\mathcal P+\epsilon'},$$
and
$$d_M\left(z_1,\exp(E^s_{(x,\omega)})\right)\ge\frac{|\pi^u_{y,x}(z_1-z_2)|}{\|\pi^u_{y,x}\|} \ge\frac{|\pi^u_{y,x}(z_1-z_2)|}{\mathcal P+\epsilon'}.$$
Since $|z_1-z_2|\le |\pi^u_{y,x}(z_1-z_2)|+|\pi^s_{y,x}(z_1-z_2)|$, without losing generality, we assume that $|\pi^s_{y,x}(z_1-z_2)|>\frac12|z_1-z_2|$. By i) of Lemma \ref{L:InvMani}, we have that
\begin{equation}\label{E:P2)1}       
|z_1-z_2|\le 2(P+\epsilon')d_M\left(z_1,\exp(E^u_{(y,\omega)})\right)\le \frac{2(P+\epsilon')}{10\mathcal P}d_M(y,z_1).
\end{equation}
Also note that
\begin{align*}
&d_M(y,z_2)\le \|\pi^s_{y,x}\|d_M(x,y)\le (\mathcal P+\epsilon')d_M(x,y),\\
&d_M(y,z_1)\le d_M(y,z_2)+|z_1-z_2|.
\end{align*}
Then we have
$$|z_1-z_2|\le \frac{2(P+\epsilon')^2}{10\mathcal P}d_M(x,y)+\frac{2(P+\epsilon')}{10\mathcal P}|z_1-z_2|,$$
which implies that
\begin{equation}\label{E:P2)2}       
|z_1-z_2|\le L_1'd_M(x,y), \text{ where }L_1'=\frac{\frac{2(P+\epsilon')^2}{10\mathcal P}}{1-\frac{2(P+\epsilon')}{10\mathcal P}}.
\end{equation}
Thus, by taking $L_1=L_1'+P+\epsilon'$, we have that
$$d_M([x,y]_\omega,y)\le |z_1-z_2|+d_M(y,z_2)\le L_1d(x,y).$$
The other part follows exactly from the same argument. Proof for P2) is completed.\\

Next, we sketch the proof for P3). Let $z_2=\exp(E^u_{(y,\omega)})\cap \exp(E^s_{(x,\omega)})$ which is the same as above and  $z_3=\exp(E^s_{(y,\omega)})\cap \exp(E^u_{(x,\omega)})$. Then we have
\begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:P3)1}       
&\left| |y-z_3|-|x-z_2|\right|\\
\le&\left||y-z_3|-|\pi^u_{(x,\omega)}(x-y)|\right|+\left||x-z_2|-|\pi^u_{(x,\omega)}(x-y)|\right|\\
=&\left||\pi^s_{x,y}(y-x)|-|\pi^u_{(x,\omega)}(x-y)|\right|+\left||\pi^s_{y,x}(y-x)|-|\pi^u_{(x,\omega)}(x-y)|\right|\\
\le &2\epsilon'|x-y|,
\end{split}
\end{align}
where $\epsilon'>0$ is a prefixed small number from (\ref{E:ErrProj}. To complete the proof of P3), we need to estimate the distance between $z_1=[x,y]_\omega$ and $z_2$ (similarly the distance betwwen $z_4:=[y,x]_\omega$ and $z_3$), which has been given by (\ref{E:P2)1}) and (\ref{E:P2)2}). The last step is to take $\delta_1>0$ small enough such that the constant "$10\mathcal P$" in (\ref{E:P2)1}) and (\ref{E:P2)2}) can be replaced by a large enough constant $K>0$ so that $L'_1<\frac14\epsilon_1$. This can be done, because of "$LipDg^\tau_{(x,\omega)}<L$" from i) and iii) of Lemma \ref{L:InvMani}. Combining with (\ref{E:P3)1}), we have that  P3) holds when we take $\epsilon'<\frac18\epsilon_1$.



                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   

 We now are ready to prove the  lemma.

 By the setting of $\phi$, there exists $L_2\ge 1$ such that the Lipschitz constants of $f_\omega$ and $f^{-1}_\omega$ are less that $L_2$ for all $\omega\in\Omega$.

Set $C_0:=\frac{(\epsilon_1+L_1)(L_2+1)}{1-\epsilon_1-(1+\epsilon_1)e^{-\lambda}}$, where we require the smallness of $\epsilon_1$ to ensure the positivity of $C_0$.
Now take $\alpha_0>0$ with $4C_0\alpha_0<\delta_1$, we will show that there exists $C\ge 1$ satisfying the required properties.

We call a subset $R_\omega\subset M_\omega$ a {\em rectangle} if its diameter is small and $[x,y]_\omega\in R_\omega$ for all $x,y\in R_\omega$. Let $A,B\subset M$ be Borel sets with diameter less than $2\epsilon$ and their Hausdorff distance are smaller than $\delta_1$. It is not hard to see that $[A,B]_\omega:=\{[x,y]_\omega|\ x\in A, y\in B\}$ is a rectangle in $M_\omega$. For a rectangle $R_\omega\subset M_\omega$, define that
$$\partial ^sR_\omega=\{x\in R_\omega:x\notin int(W^u_{\epsilon}(x,\omega)\cap R_\omega)\}$$
$$\partial ^uR_\omega=\{x\in R_\omega:x\notin int(W^s_{\epsilon}(x,\omega)\cap R_\omega)\}$$
                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                          

For a given $\alpha\in(0,\alpha_0)$, $x,y\in M_\omega$ and $z\in M_{\theta\omega}$ satisfying that $d_M(x,y)<\alpha$ and $d_M(f_\omega(x),z)<\alpha$,  we have the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item[p1)] $d_M(f_\omega(y),z)\le d_M(f_\omega(y),f_\omega(x))+d_M(f_\omega(x),z) \le (L_2+1)\alpha$.
\item[p2)]
$\max\{d_M([z,f_\omega(y)]_{\theta\omega},z),d_M([f_\omega(y),z]_{\theta\omega},y)\}\le L_1(L_2+1)\alpha$ by P2).
\item[p3)] For any $y'\in f_\omega(W^s_{C_0\alpha}(y,\omega))$, by P2), p1) and p2),
\begin{align*}
d_M([z,y']_{\theta\omega},z)
&\le d_M([z,y']_{\theta\omega},[z,f(y)]_{\theta\omega})+d_M([z,f(y)]_{\theta\omega},z)\\
&\le d_M(y',f_\omega(y))+\epsilon_1d_M(y',[z,f(y)]_{\theta\omega})+d_M([z,f(y)]_{\theta\omega},z)\\
&\le C_0\alpha e^{-\lambda}+\epsilon_1(d_M(y',f_\omega(y))+d_M(f_\omega(y),z))+L_1(L_2+1)\alpha\\
&\le (1+\epsilon_1)C_0\alpha e^{-\lambda}+(\epsilon_1+L_1)(L_2+1)\alpha\\
&= (1-\epsilon_1)C_0\alpha.
\end{align*}
\item[p4)] Similar to the arguments for p3), we have that for any $z'\in f_{\theta\omega}^{-1}(W^u_{C_0\alpha}(z,\theta\omega))$
$$ d_M([z',y]_\omega,y)\le (1-\epsilon_1)C_0\alpha.$$
\end{itemize}
Let $R_\omega(y):=\overline {[W^u_{C_0\alpha}(y,\omega),W^s_{C_0\alpha}(y,\omega)]_\omega}$. By P1) and P3), we have that for any $x\in R_\omega(y)$
\begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:DisEst1}          
d_M(x,y)&\le d_M(x,[y,x]_\omega)+d_M([y,x]_\omega,y)\\
&\le L_1d_M([x,y]_\omega,[y,x]_\omega)+C_0\alpha\\
&\le (2L_1+1)C_0\alpha.
\end{split}\end{align}
 Next, define two complete metric spaces $\mathcal V^s_\omega(y)$ and $\mathcal V^u_\omega(y)$ as follows:
$$\mathcal V^\tau_\omega(y):=\{W^\tau_{3C_0\alpha}(x,\omega)\cap R_\omega(y)|\ x\in R_\omega(y)\},\ \tau=u,s,$$
where the metric in $\mathcal V^\tau_\omega(y)$ is the Hausdorff distance.

Define a map $\mathcal F^u_\omega(y,z):\mathcal V^u_\omega(y)\to\mathcal V^u_{\theta\omega}(z)$ by letting
$$\mathcal \mathcal F^u_\omega(y,z)W=f_\omega(W)\cap R_{\theta\omega}(z),\text{ where }W\in \mathcal V^u_\omega(y).$$
By the choice of $C_0$ and p3), we can see that the above map is well defined. Moreover, p3) also implies that $\mathcal \mathcal F^u_\omega(y,z)$ is a contraction on $\mathcal V^u_\omega(y)$ with contracting rate $1-\epsilon_1$.
Similarly, we can define a contracting map $\mathcal F^s_{\theta\omega}(z,y):\mathcal V^s_{\theta\omega}(z)\to\mathcal V^s_{\omega}(y)$ by p4).\\

 Now for a given $(\omega,\alpha)$-pseudo orbit $\{(x_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ and $i,j\in\mathbb Z$ with $i<j$, define that
$$\mathcal F^u_{i,j}:=\mathcal F^u_{\theta^{j-1}\omega}(x_{j-1},x_{j})\circ\cdots\circ \mathcal F^u_{\theta^i\omega}(x_i,x_{i+1})(:\mathcal V^u_{\theta^i\omega}(x_i)\to \mathcal V^u_{\theta^j\omega}(x_j)),$$
$$\mathcal F^s_{j,i}:=\mathcal F^s_{\theta^{i+1}\omega}(x_{i+1},x_{i})\circ\cdots\circ \mathcal F^s_{\theta^j\omega}(x_j,x_{i-1})(:\mathcal V^s_{\theta^j\omega}(x_j)\to \mathcal V^s_{\theta^i\omega}(x_i)),$$
which are both contractions. Thus the following set consists of only one point which is denoted by $y_i$
  $$\lim_{k\to\infty}\left(\mathcal F^u_{i-k,i}\left(V^u_{\theta^{i-k}\omega}(x_{i-k})\right)\cap \mathcal F^s_{i+k,i}\left(V^s_{\theta^{i+k}\omega}(x_{i+k})\right)\right).$$
  It is clear that $\{(y_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$ is a true orbit and $y_i\in R_{\theta^i\omega}(x_i)$. Therefore, (\ref{E:DisEst1}) tells that taking $C=(2L_1+1)C_0$ will fit the need.

label: L:ContinousShadowing
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:ContinousShadowing}                     
For a given $\beta\in(0,\beta_0)$, let $\alpha\in (0,\alpha_0)$ be as in   Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing} corresponding to $\beta$ where $\alpha_0$ is as in Lemma  \ref{L:ClosingLemma}.  Then for any $\tau>0$, there exists $N_0\in\mathbb N$ such that given any  two $(\omega,\alpha)$-pseudo orbits $\{(x_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ and $\{(x_i',\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ which are $(\omega,\beta)$-shadowed by two uniquely defined true orbits $\{(y_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ and $\{(y_i',\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ respectively, for any $N>N_0$ if $x_i=x_i',\ \forall i\in[-N,N]$, then $d_M(y_0,y_0')<\tau$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that if $x_i=x_i',\ \forall i\in[-N,N]$, then $d_M(y_i,y_i')<2\beta,\ \forall i\in[-N,N]$.  Let $z=[y_0,y'_0]_\omega$, where $[\cdot,\cdot]_\cdot$ is defined in \ref{L:LocCoor} for a fixed $\delta$ corresponding to $\epsilon=\frac12\epsilon_0$. By the definition of local unstable manifold and ii) of Lemma \ref{L:InvMani}, we have that
\begin{align*}
d_M(z,y'_0)&\le e^{-N\lambda}d_M(\pi_M\phi^N(z,\omega),y_N')\\
&\le e^{-N\lambda}(d_M(y_N,y'_N)+d_M(\pi_M\phi^N(z,\omega),y_N))\\
&\le e^{-N\lambda}(2\beta+d_M(z,y_0))\\
&\le e^{-N\lambda}(2\beta+\frac12\epsilon_0).
\end{align*}
The same argument is applicable to $d_M(z,y_0)$ if we reverse the time. Therefore,
$$d_M(y_0,y'_0)\le  2L_1e^{-N\lambda}(2\beta+\frac12\epsilon_0),$$
where $L_1$ is a constant given by P2) at beginning of the proof of Lemma  \ref{L:ClosingLemma}.
The proof is completed.

label: L:LShad
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:LShad}        
For any $\beta\in(0,\beta_0)$, there exists an $\alpha>0$ such that for any $\alpha$-pseudo orbit $\{g'_i\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$, there is a unique true orbit $\{g_i\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$ of $\tilde\phi$ such that
$$\sup_{i\in \mathbb Z}d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(g_i,g'_i)<\beta,$$
where $\beta_0$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing}, and
$\{g_i\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$ is called {\bf $\beta$-shadowing} orbit of $\{g'_i\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$.

Moreover,  there exist an $\alpha_0>0$ and $C\ge 1$ so that for any $\alpha\in (0,\alpha_0)$ and any $\alpha$-pseudo orbit $\{g'_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$, there exists a true orbit $\{g_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ of $\tilde\phi$ satisfying the following
$$\sup_{i\in \mathbb Z} d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(g_i,g'_i)<C\alpha.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we note that each $\alpha$-pseudo orbit $\{g'_i\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$ induces an $(\omega,\alpha)$-pseudo orbit \[\{(g'_i(\theta^i\omega),\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}\]
for each $\omega\in \Omega$. Thus Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing} is applicable and produces a map $g:\Omega\to M$ such that $\{(g(\theta^i\omega),\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$ is $(\omega,\beta)$-shadowing $\{(g_i(\theta^i\omega),\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are as in Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing}. Once $g$ is Borel measurable, the proof follows from Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing} and \ref{L:ClosingLemma}.

Next, we prove that $g$ is Borel measurable. For $h\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ and $r>0$, denote $B_\Omega(h,r)$ the open tubular neighborhood of $graph(h)$, i.e.,
$$B_\Omega(h,r):=\left\{(x,\omega)|\ \omega\in\Omega, d_M(x,h(\omega))<r\right\}.$$
It is not hard to see that $B_\Omega(h,r)$ is a Borel subset of $M\times\Omega$. In fact, since $M$ is compact, there exists a sequence of simple functions $\{h_i:\Omega\to M\}_{i\in \mathbb N}$ such that
$$d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(h_i,h)<\frac{r}{i+2},\ i\in \mathbb N.$$
Note that each $B_\Omega(h_i,\frac{ir}{i+2})$ is a Borel subset of $M\times\Omega$ because it is a union of finite rectangle sets, thus $B_\Omega(h,r)=\cup_{i\in N}B_\Omega(h_i,\frac{ir}{i+2})$ implies the Borel measurability of  $B_\Omega(h,r)$.

Coming back to $g$ and $g_i'$, by the uniqueness of $g$, we have that
$$graph(g)=\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\phi^{-i}\left(B_\Omega(g_i,\beta)\right).$$
For $k\in\mathbb N$, let $$S_k:=\bigcap_{i\in[-k,k]\cap \mathbb Z}\phi^{-i}\left(B_\Omega(g_i,\beta)\right).$$
By the continuity of $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$, $S_k$ is a Borel subset in $M\times\Omega$. Also note that for each $\omega\in\Omega$,
$$S_k\cap M_\omega=\bigcap_{i\in[-k,k]\cap \mathbb Z}\pi_M\phi^{-i}\left(\left\{(x,\theta^i\omega)|\ d_M(x,g_i(\theta^i\omega))<\beta\right\}\right),$$
which is a nonempty open subset of $M_\omega$. By applying Theorem \ref{T:BMST} to each $S_k$, we have that for each $k\in\mathbb N$, there exists a Borel measurable map $g_k:\Omega\to M$ such that
$$graph(g_k)\subset S_k.$$
By the uniqueness of $g$ and Lemma \ref{L:Expansive}, we have that $$\lim_{k\to\infty}\sup_{\omega\in\Omega}\{d_M(g_k(\omega),g(\omega)\}=0,$$
which implies that $g$ is Borel measurable. The proof is completed.

body_md:
\label{L:LContShad}            
Let $\alpha_0$ and  $\beta_0$ are as in Lemma  \ref{L:LShad}, and for a given $\beta\in(0,\beta_0)$, $\alpha\in (0,\alpha_0)$ be the one as in  Lemma \ref{L:LShad} corresponding to $\beta$.   Then for any $\tau>0$, there exists $N_0\in\mathbb N$ such that the following holds: given any  two $\alpha$-pseudo orbits $\{g_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ and $\{g_i'\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ of $\tilde \phi$, which are $\beta$-shadowed by two true orbits $\{\tilde g_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ and $\{\tilde g_i'\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ respectively, then for any $N>N_0$, $g_i=g_i',\ \forall i\in[-N,N]$, we have that

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Firstly, fix a given Borel function $g\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ and $\epsilon>0$. Without losing  generality, we assume that $\epsilon<\frac12\beta_0$, where $\beta_0$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing} and \ref{L:LShad}. Taking $\beta=\frac13\epsilon$ and applying Lemma \ref{L:LShad}, there exists $\alpha>0$ corresponding to $\beta$ as in Lemma \ref{L:LShad}. Again, for the sake of convenience, we assume that $\alpha<\beta$.
By the compactness of $M$, there exists  a finite open cover $\{U_i,1\le i\le n_0\}$ of which each $U_i=B(x_i,\frac13\alpha)$ is a ball of radius $\alpha$ in $M$.

Secondly, define a function $k:\Omega\to \{1,2,\cdots, n_0\}$ by the following
\begin{equation}\label{E:MeasurableIndex}                  
k(\omega)=\min\left\{i\in \{1,\cdots,n_0\}\big|\ g(\omega)\in U_i\right\},\ \forall \omega\in\Omega.
\end{equation}
It is not hard to see that $k$ is a measurable  function since $g$ is measurable and the following holds
\begin{align*}
&\left\{\omega|\ k(\omega)=i\right\}\\
=&\begin{cases}
\{\omega|\ g(\omega)\in U_i\}&\text{ when } i=1\\
\{\omega|\ g(\omega)\in U_i\}\setminus\left(\bigcup_{1\le j\le i-1}\{\omega|\ g(\omega)\in U_j\}\right)&\text{ when } i\in\{2,\cdots, n_0\}
\end{cases}.
\end{align*}
This Borel measurable function $k(\omega)$ induces a finite measurable partition of $\Omega$,
$$\left\{\Omega_i:=\{\omega|\ k(\omega)=i\}\right\}_{i\in\{1,\cdots,n_0\}}.$$
Note that, by condition H2), there exists $N\in\mathbb N$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{E:MixingTimeS2}               
\pi_M\phi^n(U_i,\omega)\cap U_j\neq \emptyset,\ \forall \omega\in \Omega, i,j\in\{1,\cdots,n_0\},n\ge N.
\end{equation}
Then, for any $n\ge N$, $k$ and $n$ induces a finite measurable partition of $\Omega$, $\{\Omega^{n}_{ij}\}_{i,j\in\{1,\cdots,n_0\}}$, by letting
$$\Omega^n_{ij}:=\left\{\omega\big|\ k(\omega)=i, k(\theta^n\omega)=j\right\}=\theta^{-n}(\Omega_j)\cap \Omega_i.$$
By the uniform continuity of $\phi$, there exists $\delta_1>0$ such that the following holds
\begin{equation}\label{E:CondDelt1}            
d_M(\pi_M\phi(x,\omega_1),\pi_M\phi(x,\omega_2))<\frac16\alpha,\ \forall x\in M\text{ and } d_\Omega(\omega_1,\omega_2)<\delta_1.
\end{equation}
Additionally, by the uniform continuity of $\theta$, for a fixed $n\ge N$, there exists $\delta_2>0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{E:CondDelt2}            
d_\Omega(\theta^m\omega_1,\theta^m\omega_2)<\delta_1\ \forall0\le m\le  n-1 \text{ and  }d_\Omega(w_1,w_2)<\delta_2.
\end{equation}
Now take a finite measurable partition of $\Omega$, $\{\Omega'_s\}_{s\in S}$, which is taken to be a refinement of $\{\Omega^n_{ij}\}_{i,j\in\{1,\cdots,n_0\}}$ and has diameter less than $\delta_2$. By (\ref{E:MixingTimeS2}), we have that for any $\omega\in\Omega^n_{ij}$, there exists an $x\in U_i$ such that  $\phi^n(x,\omega)\in (U_j,t^n\omega)$.
Then, for each $\Omega'_s(\subset \Omega^n_{ij})$, arbitrarily fix a point $(y_s,\omega_s)\in U_i\times \Omega'_s$ such that
 $$\pi_M\phi^n(y_s,\omega_s)\in U_j.$$
Define a simple function $y=\sum_{s\in S}y_s\chi_{\Omega'_s}$, where $\chi_{\Omega'_s}$ is the characteristic function of $\Omega'_s$. \\

Now, we are ready to construct the $(\omega,\alpha)$-pseudo-orbits which visit the tubular neighborhood of $graph(g)$ periodically (with period of $n$).  For a given $\omega\in\Omega$, denote $q_\omega:\mathbb Z\to S$ the function satisfying that for any $l\in \mathbb Z$, $\theta^{ln}(\omega)\in \Omega_{q(l)}'$. Then define
\begin{equation}\label{E:DefPseOrbS2)}               
y'_i(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
y(\theta^{ln}\omega),&\text{when } i=ln\\
\pi_M\left(\phi^{i-ln}(y(\theta^{ln}\omega),\omega_{q_\omega(l)})\right),&\text{when }i\in[ln+1,(l+1)n-1]
\end{cases},
\end{equation}
where the map $y'_i:\Omega\to M$ is clearly Borel measurable.
For $l\in\mathbb Z$ and $i\in  [ln,(l+1)n-1]$, by the choice of $\delta_2$ and (\ref{E:CondDelt2}), we have that
$$d_\Omega(\theta^{i}\omega,\theta^{i-ln}\omega_{q_\omega(l)})<\delta_1.$$
Therefore, by (\ref{E:CondDelt1}), we have that, for $i\in  [ln,(l+1)n-2]$
\begin{align*}
&d_M\left(\pi_M\phi(y_i'(\omega)),y_{i+1}'(\omega)\right)\\
=&d_M\left(\pi_M\phi\left(\pi_M\phi^{i-ln}(y(\theta^{ln}\omega),\omega_{q_\omega(l)}),\theta^i\omega\right),\pi_M\phi\left(\pi_M\phi^{i-ln}(y(\theta^{ln}\omega),\omega_{q_\omega(l)}),\theta^i\omega_{q_\omega(l)}\right)\right)\\
\le&\frac16\alpha,
\end{align*}
and for $i=(l+1)n-1$,
\begin{align*}
&d_M\left(\pi_M\phi(y'_{(l+1)n-1}(\omega),\theta^{(l+1)n-1}\omega),y'_{(l+1)n}(\omega)\right)\\
\le &d_M\left(\pi_M\phi\left(\pi_M\phi^{i-ln}(y(\theta^{ln}\omega),\omega_{q_\omega(l)}),\theta^i\omega\right),\pi_M\phi\left(\pi_M\phi^{i-ln}(y(\theta^{ln}\omega),\omega_{q_\omega(l)}),\theta^i\omega_{q_\omega(l)}\right)\right)\\
&+d_M\left(\pi_M\phi^{N}(y(\theta^{ln}\omega),\omega_{q_\omega(l)}),y(\theta^{(l+1)n}\omega)\right)\\
<&\frac16\alpha+\frac23\alpha<\alpha.
\end{align*}
In the above estimate, we used the fact that $\phi^{n}(y(\theta^{ln}\omega),\omega_{q_\omega(l)})$ and $y(\theta^{(l+1)n}\omega)$  fall in a same element of  $\{U_i\}_{i\in\{1,\cdots,n_0\}}$. This conclude that $\{(y'_i\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ forms an $\alpha$-pseudo orbit of $\tilde\phi$. Thus, by Lemma \ref{L:LShad}, there exists a unique true orbit $\{\tilde\phi^i(\tilde g), \tilde g\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ which is $\beta$-shadowing  $\{y'_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$. Note that $\{\phi^i(\tilde g)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ and $\{\phi^{i+n}(\tilde g)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ are two true orbits and
$$d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(\tilde\phi^{i+n}(\tilde g),\tilde\phi^i(\tilde g))\le 2\beta<\frac13\beta_0,\ \forall i\in \mathbb Z.$$
Then Lemma \ref{L:LContShad} implies that
$$\tilde\phi^n(\tilde g)=\tilde g\ i.e.\ \phi^{n} (graph(\tilde g))=graph(\tilde g).$$
This completes the proof of this theorem.  \qed

label: L:AlDefH
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that the original definition of $\underline h(M\times \Omega|\Omega)$ is given by
$$\underline h(M\times \Omega|\Omega)=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\epsilon,n).$$
This lemma simply states that the above order of $\inf$ and $\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}$ can be exchanged. First, we clearly have that
$$\underline h(M\times \Omega|\Omega)=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\epsilon,n)\ge\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\epsilon,n).$$
Next, we show that the opposite inequality also holds. To see this, we claim

\noindent
{\bf Claim}:{\it  There exists $\eta >0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{E:ConstantEta}              
h_{top}(\phi|M_\omega):=\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\epsilon,n)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\eta,n),\ \forall \omega\in\Omega.
\end{equation}}
\noindent{\em Proof of the Claim}: It is obvious that $h_{top}(\phi|M_\omega)\ge \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\eta,n)$ by definition. Hence, it remains to prove the opposite inequality.

Firstly, we fix an $\eta>0$ satisfying the following property: for any $x,y\in M_\omega$
$$\sup_{n\in\mathbb Z}d(\phi^n(x,\omega),\phi^n(y,\omega))\le \eta\;\text{ implies }\;x=y.$$
The existence of such $\eta$ follows from the expansive property of $\phi$, where one only requires $\eta<\epsilon$ for the $\epsilon$ from Lemma \ref{L:Expansive}.

Secondly, by Lemma \ref{L:ContinousShadowing}, we have that for any $\epsilon'\in(0,\eta)$, there exists $L(\epsilon')\in \mathbb N$ such that for any $x,y\in M_\omega$
\begin{equation}\label{E:SepControl}             
\max_{|n|\le L(\epsilon')}d(\phi^n(x,\omega),\phi^n(y,\omega))\le \eta\text{ implies }d_M(x,y)<\epsilon'.
\end{equation}
By (\ref{E:SepControl}), we have for any $\omega\in\Omega$, $n\in\mathbb N$, and $x,y\in M_\omega$,
$$d^\phi_{M\times \Omega,n+2L(\epsilon')}((x,\omega),(y,\omega))\le \eta\text{ implies }d^\phi_{M\times \Omega,n}(\phi^{L(\epsilon')}(x,\omega),\phi^{L(\epsilon')}(y,\omega))<\epsilon',$$
which yields
\begin{equation}\label{E:SepNEst1}           
N(\theta^{L(\epsilon')}\omega,\epsilon',n)\le N(\omega,\eta,n+2L(\epsilon')),\ \forall \omega\in\Omega, n\in \mathbb N, \epsilon'\in(0,\eta).
\end{equation}
Note that
\begin{equation}\label{E:SepNEst2}           
N(\omega,\epsilon',n+m)\le N(\omega,\epsilon',m)N(\theta^m\omega,\epsilon',n).
\end{equation}
(\ref{E:SepNEst1}) and (\ref{E:SepNEst2}) imply that
\begin{align*}
h_{top}(\phi|M_\omega)=&\lim_{\epsilon'\to0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\epsilon',n)\\
=&\lim_{\epsilon'\to0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1{n+L(\epsilon')}\log N(\omega,\epsilon',n+L(\epsilon'))\\
\le&\lim_{\epsilon'\to0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1{n+L(\epsilon')}\left(\log N(\omega,\epsilon',L(\epsilon'))+\log N(\theta^{L(\epsilon')}\omega,\epsilon',n)\right)\\
\le&\lim_{\epsilon'\to0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1{n+L(\epsilon')}\left(\log N(\omega,\epsilon',L(\epsilon'))+\log N(\omega,\eta,n+2L(\epsilon'))\right)\\
=&\lim_{\epsilon'\to0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1{n+L(\epsilon')}\log N(\omega,\eta,n+2L(\epsilon'))\\
=&\lim_{\epsilon'\to0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1{n}\log N(\omega,\eta,n)\\
=&\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1{n}\log N(\omega,\eta,n).
\end{align*}
Therfore (\ref{E:ConstantEta}) holds, which yields
\begin{align*}
\underline h(M\times \Omega|\Omega)=&\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\epsilon,n)\\
=&\inf_{\omega\in \Omega} h_{top}(\phi|M_\omega)\\
=&\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\eta,n)\\
\le &\lim_{\eta\to0^+}\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\eta,n),
\end{align*}
which completes the proof of this lemma.

label: L:Horseshoe
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:Horseshoe}            
If $\phi$ satisfies condition H1) and H2), then for any $k\in \mathbb N\setminus\{1\}$ there exists $N\in \mathbb N$ such that $\phi^N$ has a $k$-symbol strong full random horseshoe.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\{x_i\}_{1\le i\le k}$ be an $3\epsilon$-separated finite subset of $M$. Such a set exists for small enough $\epsilon>0$, and we fix this $\epsilon$.  Without loss of  generality, we assume that $\epsilon<\frac12\beta_0$, where $\beta_0$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:LShad}. For $\beta=\frac13\epsilon$,  there exists an $\alpha>0$ corresponding to $\beta$ as in Lemma \ref{L:LShad}. Again, for the sake  of convenience, we assume that $\alpha<\beta$. For any $i\in \{1,\cdots,k\}$, let $U_i=B(x_i,\frac13\alpha)$.

By Condition H2), there exists an $N\in\mathbb N$ such that the following holds
\begin{equation}\label{E:MixingTimeS2S}                
\pi_M\phi^n(U_i,\omega)\cap U_j\neq \emptyset,\ \forall \omega\in \Omega, i,j\in\{1,\cdots,k\},n\ge N.
\end{equation}
By the uniform continuity of $\phi$ and $\theta$, there exist $\delta_1,\delta_2>0$ such that (\ref{E:CondDelt1}) and (\ref{E:CondDelt2}) hold. Let $\{\Omega_s'\}_{s\in S}$ be a finite Borel measurable partition of $\Omega$ with diameter less than $\delta_2$. By (\ref{E:MixingTimeS2S}), for any $s\in S$ and $i,j\in\{1\cdots,k\}$, there exists $(y^{i,j}_s,\omega^{i,j}_s)\in U_i\times \Omega'_s$ such that
$$\pi_M\phi^N(y^{i,j}_s,\omega^{i,j}_s)\in U_j.$$
We define a simple function $y^{i,j}=\sum_{s\in S}y^{i,j}_s\chi_{\Omega'_s}$ for all $i,j\in\{1,\cdots,k\}$.

Now, we are ready to build the strong random horseshoe by constructing a proper $\alpha$-pseudo-orbits of $\tilde\phi$ associated to elements from $\mathcal S_k:=\{1,\cdots, k\}^{\mathbb Z}$.

For a given $\hat a=(a_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}\in \mathcal S_k$, and a given $\omega\in\Omega$, we denote $q_\omega:\mathbb Z\to S$ the function satisfying that for any $l\in \mathbb Z$, $\theta^{lN}(\omega)\in \Omega_{q(l)}'$. Then, we define
\begin{equation}\label{E:DefPseOrbS2)}               
y'_{\hat a,\omega}(i)=
\begin{cases}
y^{a_l,a_{l+1}}(\theta^{lN}\omega),&\text{when } i=lN\\
\pi_M\left(\phi^{i-lN}(y^{a_l,a_{l+1}}(\theta^{lN}\omega),\omega^{a_l,a_{l+1}}_{q_\omega(l)})\right),&\text{when }i\in[lN+1,(l+1)N-1]
\end{cases}.
\end{equation}
Set $$g_i(\omega):=y'_{\hat a,\omega}(i),\ \forall \omega\in\Omega,\ i\in \mathbb Z.$$
It is clear that each $g_i:\Omega\to M$ is Borel measurable since $g_i$ is either a simple function or the image of a simple function under $\phi$ or $\phi^{-1}$'s iterations.

For $l\in\mathbb Z$ and $i\in  [lN,(l+1)N-1]$, by the choice of $\delta_2$ and (\ref{E:CondDelt2}), we have that
$$d_\Omega(\theta^{i}\omega,\theta^{i-lN}\omega^{a_l,a_{l+1}}_{q_\omega(l)})<\delta_1.$$
Therefore, by (\ref{E:CondDelt1}), we have that, for $i\in  [lN,(l+1)N-2]$, \\
(to save space, let $z=\pi_M\phi^{i-lN}\left(y^{a_l,a_{l+1}}(\theta^{lN}\omega),\omega^{a_l,a_{l+1}}_{q_\omega(l)}\right)$)
\begin{align*}
&d_M\left(\pi_M\phi(y'_{\hat a,\omega}(i)),y'_{\hat a,\omega}(i+1)\right)
=d_M\left(\pi_M\phi\left(z,\theta^i\omega\right),\pi_M\phi\left(z,\theta^i\omega^{a_l,a_{l+1}}_{q_\omega(l)}\right)\right)
\le\frac16\alpha,
\end{align*}
while for $i=(l+1)N-1$,
\begin{align*}
&d_M\left(\pi_M\phi(y'_{\hat a,\omega}(i),\theta^{i}\omega),y'_{\hat a,\omega}(i+1)\right)\\
\le &d_M\left(\pi_M\phi\left(z,\theta^i\omega\right),\pi_M\phi\left(z,\theta^i\omega^{a_l,a_{l+1}}_{q_\omega(l)}\right)\right)\\
&+d_M\left(\pi_M\phi^{N}(y^{a_l,a_{l+1}}(\theta^{lN}\omega),\omega^{a_l,a_{l+1}}_{q_\omega(l)}),y^{a_{l+1},a_{l+2}}(\theta^{(l+1)N}\omega)\right)\\
<&\frac16\alpha+\frac23\alpha<\alpha.
\end{align*}
                                                                                                                                                                                  
 This concludes that for any $\omega\in \Omega$, $\{(y'_{\hat,\omega}(i),\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ forms an $(\omega,\alpha)$-pseudo orbit of $\phi$. Thus $\{g_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ forms an $\alpha$-pseudo orbit of $\tilde \phi$. Thereafter, Lemma \ref{L:LShad} implies the existence of a unique true orbit $\{\phi^i(\tilde )\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ which is $\beta$-shadowing  $\{g_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$.

 We define the map $\Psi:\mathcal S_k\to L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ by letting
$$\Psi(\hat a)=g_{\hat a},\ \forall \hat a\in \mathcal S_k.$$
 where the continuity of $\Psi$ follows from Lemma \ref{L:LContShad}.


 Note that $\{\tilde\phi^i(\tilde g_{\hat a})\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ and $\{\tilde\phi^i(\tilde g_{\sigma \hat a})\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ are two true orbits and
$$d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(\tilde\phi^{i+N}(\tilde g),\tilde\phi^i(\tilde g_{\sigma\hat a})\le 2\beta<\frac13\beta_0,$$
therefore, by Lemma \ref{L:LContShad}, we have that
$$\tilde\phi^N(\tilde g_{\hat a})=(\tilde g_{\sigma\hat a} )\ i.e.\ \phi^{N} graph(\tilde g_{\hat a})=graph(\tilde g_{\sigma\hat a}),$$
which implies (ii) in Definition \ref{D:SRandomHorseshoe}.




 Now we prove i) in Definition \ref{D:SRandomHorseshoe}. For any $\hat a_1=(a_1(i))_{i\in \mathbb Z},\hat a_2=(a_2(i))_{i\in \mathbb Z}\in\mathcal S_k$ with $\hat a_1\neq \hat a_2$, let $s=\min\{|i||\ a_1(i)\neq a_2(i)\}$. Then,  by the choice of $x_i,U_i,\epsilon,\alpha,\beta$ at the beginning of this section,  we have that
 \begin{equation}\label{E:SepSym}         
 d^{\phi}_{M\times\Omega,N}\left(\phi^{rN}(\Psi(\hat a_1)(\omega),\omega),\phi^{rN}(\Psi(\hat a_2)(\omega),\omega)\right)>\epsilon,\ \forall\omega\in\Omega,
 \end{equation}
 where $a_1(r)\neq a_2(r)$ with $|r|=s$ and $d^{\phi}_{M\times\Omega,N}$ is the Bowen metric. Note that there is a constant $L>1$ such that for any $\omega\in\Omega$ and $x,y\in M$ with $d(x,y)>0$, we have
 $$d(\phi^{\pm1}(x,\omega),\phi^{\pm1}(y,\omega))\le Ld_M(x,y).$$
 Therefore
 \begin{equation}\label{E:SHorsSeparation}                  
 d_M\left(\pi_M\left(\Psi(\hat a_1)(\omega),\omega\right),\pi_M\phi^{rN}\left(\Psi(\hat a_2)(\omega),\omega\right)\right)>\epsilon L^{-N},\ \forall\omega\in\Omega,
\end{equation}
which implies Condition i) of Definition \ref{D:SRandomHorseshoe} by taking $\Delta =\epsilon L^{-N}$.

 Finally, the continuity of $\Psi^{-1}$ can be obtained by the following estimate:
 \begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:PsiInverseContinuity}
& d_M(\Psi(\hat a_1)(\omega),\Psi(\hat a_2)(\omega))\\
=&d\left((\Psi(\hat a_1)(\omega),\omega),(\Psi(\hat a_2)(\omega),\omega)\right)\\
\ge& L^{-|rN|}d\left(\phi^{rN}(\Psi(\hat a_1)(\omega),\omega),\phi^{rN}(\Psi(\hat a_2)(\omega),\omega)\right)\\
\ge& \epsilon L^{-(s+1)N}.
\end{split}
 \end{align}
 The proof is completed.

label: E:SepNEst
title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{L:AlDefH}, we have that there exists $\epsilon'_0>0$ such that for any $\epsilon'\in(0,\epsilon'_0)$ the following holds
\begin{equation}\label{E:SepNEst}          
\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\epsilon',n)>\underline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\frac14\gamma.
\end{equation}

Let $\epsilon'_1=\min\left\{\frac12\beta_0,\epsilon'_0\right\}$, where $\beta_0$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:LShad}. Taking $\beta=\frac16\epsilon'_1$, there exists an $\alpha>0$ corresponding to $\beta$ as in Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing}. Again, for the sake  of convenience, we assume that $\alpha<\beta$. Now we fix an $\epsilon\in(0,\beta)$, and also fix a set of open balls in $M$ with radius equaling $\min\{\frac13\alpha,\frac16\epsilon\}$, $\{U_i,0\le i\le p\}$, where $\{U_i\}_{1\le i\le p}$ forms an open cover of $M$.

By Condition H2), there exists $N_1\in\mathbb N$ such that the following holds
\begin{equation}\label{E:MixingLS}           
\pi_M\phi^n(U_i,\omega)\cap U_j\neq \emptyset,\ \forall \omega\in \Omega, i,j\in\{0,1,\cdots,p\},n\ge N_1.
\end{equation}





By (\ref{E:SepNEst}) and $\beta\le \frac16 \epsilon_0'$, for any $\omega\in\Omega$, there exist $l(\omega),m(\omega)\in \mathbb N$, and a $3\beta$-separated set $\{z_i(\omega)\}_{1\le i\le l(\omega)}$ with respect to $d^\phi_{M\times \Omega,m(\omega)}$ satisfies that
\begin{equation}\label{E:SepNEstO}            
\frac{1}{m(\omega)+2N_1}\log l(\omega)>\underline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\frac12\gamma.
\end{equation}
Since $\phi$ is continuous and $\Omega$ is compact, the $3\beta$-separated set can be chosen properly to make $m(\omega)$ being uniformly bounded on $\Omega$. The bound is denoted by $N_2$. Let $N=L(N_2+2N_1)$, where $L$ is a prefixed large positive integer.

Note that, by the choice of $\alpha$ and $\beta$, if two $(\omega,\alpha)$-pseudo orbits have a $3\beta$-separation on time $n$, then the corresponding true orbits which are $(\omega,\beta)$-shadowing them respectively  have a $\beta$-separation on time $n$. Therefore, here instead of constructing specific pseudo orbits, we would like to count the number of  $(\omega,\frac23\alpha)$-pseudo orbits which have $3\beta$-separations happened during time interval $[0,N]$.


 First, we describe the procedure defining the pseudo orbits. For a given $\omega\in\Omega$, by (\ref{E:MixingLS}), we can use a segment of a true orbit to connect $(U_0,\omega)$ to any one of $\{(U_i,\theta^{N_1})\}_{1\le i\le p}$. This orbit segment of connecting $U_0$ to some $U_i$ is the first piece of the $(\omega,\frac23\alpha)$-pseudo orbit. The second piece of the  $(\omega,\frac23\alpha)$-pseudo orbit is one of the orbit segments \[\{\phi^j(z_i(\theta^{N_1}\omega),\theta^{N_1}\omega)\}_{0\le j\le m(\theta^{N_1}\omega)-1}
  \]which is a segment of a true orbit. So in order to ensure that these two pieces can be merged with variation $\le \frac23\alpha$, $U_i$ chosen in the first step should contains the $z_i(\theta^{N_1}\omega)$ chosen in the second step. The third piece of these $(\omega,\frac23\alpha)$-pseudo orbits is to connect $\phi^{m(\theta^{N_1}\omega)}(z_i(\theta^{N_1}\omega),\theta^{N_1}\omega)$ to $U_0$ by a true orbit segment with length $N_1$, which can be done again by (\ref{E:MixingLS}). We repeat this procedure and  derive a sequence of integers in the following way
 \begin{align*}
 R_0&=0\\
 R_1&=2N_1+m(\theta^{N_1}\omega)\\
R_2&=2N_1+m(\theta^{R_1+N_1}\omega)\\
&\cdots\\
R_{n+1}&=2N_1+m(\theta^{\sum_{i=1}^nR_i+N_1}\omega)\\
&\cdots
 \end{align*}
Let $$s:=\max\left\{n\Big|\ \sum_{i=1}^nR_i\le (L-1)(N_2+2N_1)\right\}.$$
 The above procedure of constructing pseudo orbits repeats $s$ times in the time interval $[0,\sum_{i=1}^sR_i]$. For the time interval $[\sum_{i=1}^sR_i,N]$, we use only one orbit segment to connect $(U_0,\theta^{\sum_{i=1}^sR_i}\omega)$ to $(U_0,\theta^{N}\omega)$. It is not hard to see that the number of $(\omega,\frac23\alpha)$-pseudo orbits which are $3\beta$-separated in the time interval $[0,N]$ is
 $$K(\omega)=\prod_{i=1}^sl\left(\theta^{\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}R_j+N_1}\omega\right).$$
 Let $N_3=N-\sum_{i=1}^sR_i$, then $N_3\le 2(N_2+2N_1)$. Therefore, by (\ref{E:SepNEstO}), we have that
 \begin{align*}
 &\frac{\log K(\omega)}N\\
 =&\frac{\sum_{i=1}^s\log l\left(\theta^{\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}R_j+N_1}\omega\right)}N\\
 \ge&\frac{\left(\underline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\frac12\gamma\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^s\left(m\left(\theta^{\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}R_j+N_1}\omega\right)+2N_1\right)\right)}N\\
 =&\left(\underline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\frac12\gamma\right)\frac{{\sum_{i=1}^sR_i}}N=\left(\underline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\frac12\gamma\right)\frac{N-N_3}N\\
  \ge&\left(\underline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\frac12\gamma\right)\left(1-\frac2L\right).
 \end{align*}
The largeness of $L$ is to ensure the  following
$$\frac{\log K(\omega)}N>\underline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\gamma.$$
For any given $\omega\in \Omega$, let $\{y_j(\theta^i\omega)\}_{0\le i\le N-1}$, $1\le j\le K(\omega)$, be the segments of $(\omega,\frac23\alpha)$-pseudo orbits of $\phi$ defined above. By the uniform continuous of $\phi$, there exist $\delta_1,\delta_2>$ such that (\ref{E:CondDelt1}) and (\ref{E:CondDelt2}) hold, where $n$ in (\ref{E:CondDelt2}) is replaced by $N$. Let $\{\Omega_s'\}_{s\in S}$ be a finite Borel measurable partition of $\Omega$ with diameter less than $\delta_2$. We fix an $\omega'_s\in \Omega'_s$ for each $s\in S$, and let $K=\min\{K(\omega'_s)\}_{s\in S}$. Note that we
$$\frac{\log K}N>\underline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\gamma.$$
Define the simple functions as follows
$$g_{i,j}=\sum_{s\in S}y_j(\theta^i\omega_s')\chi_{\theta^i(\Omega'_s)},\ 0\le i\le N-1,\ 1\le j\le K.$$
where $\chi_{\theta^i(\Omega'_s)}$ is the characteristic function of $\theta^i(\Omega'_s)$. It is not hard to see that (\ref{E:CondDelt1}) and (\ref{E:CondDelt2}) imply that
\begin{equation}\label{E:SimpFuncShd1}               
d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(\tilde\phi(g_{i,j}),g_{i+1,j})\le d_M(y_j(\theta^i\omega'_s),y_j(\theta^{i+1}\omega'_s)+\frac16\alpha<\alpha,\ 0\le i\le N-2,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{E:SimpFuncShd2}               
d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(\tilde\phi(g_{N-1,j}),g_{0,j'})\le \text{ diameter of }U_0+\frac16\alpha<\alpha,\ 1\le j,j'\le K.
\end{equation}
Also note that for $1\le j,j'\le K$ with $j\neq j'$ and each $\omega\in\Omega$, $\{y_j(\theta^i\omega)\}_{0\le i\le N-1}$ and $\{y_{j'}(\theta^i\omega)\}_{0\le i\le N-1}$ are $3\beta$-separated with respect to $d^\phi_{M\times \Omega,m(\omega)}$, thus we have that
\begin{equation}\label{E:SHorsSepa}            
\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}\max_{0\le i\le N-1}d_M(g_{i,j}(\omega), g_{i,j'}(\omega))\ge 3\beta.
\end{equation}

Now, we are ready to construct the strong full random horseshoe.

For $\hat a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}\in \mathcal S_k$, let
\begin{equation}\label{E:SHorsPsOr}            
 g^{\hat a}_i=g_{i-\left[\frac iN\right]N,a_{\left[\frac iN\right]}},\ i\in \mathbb Z,
\end{equation}
where $\left[\frac iN\right]$ is the largest integer less than $\frac iN$. By (\ref{E:SimpFuncShd1}) and (\ref{E:SimpFuncShd2}), we have that $\{ g^{\hat a}_i\}_{1\in\mathbb Z}$ forms an $\alpha$-pseudo orbit of $\tilde \phi$, thus Lemma \ref{L:LShad} implies a true orbit of $\tilde \phi$, $ \{\tilde\phi^i(g^{\hat a})\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$, which is $\beta$-shadowing $\{ g^{\hat a}_i\}_{1\in\mathbb Z}$.

Define $\Psi:\mathcal S_k\to L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ by letting
$$\Psi(\hat a)=g^{\hat a},$$where the continuity of $\Psi$ follows from  Lemma \ref{L:LContShad} immediately.
It is obvious that (\ref{E:SHorsSepa}) and the argument for (\ref{E:SHorsSeparation}) imply Condition i) of Definition \ref{D:SRandomHorseshoe} with $\Delta=\beta L^{-N}$. ii) of Definition and the continuity of $\Psi^{-1}$ follow exactly from the same arguments as (\ref{E:PsiInverseContinuity}), thus we do not repeat it here.
This completes the proof of Part A. of Theorem \ref{T:TheoryAnosovMix2}.

name: Proof of Part A. of Theorem \ref{T:TheoryAnosovMix2}

title: Proof
body_md:
For a given $\gamma>0$, by the definition of $\overline h(M\times \Omega|\Omega)$, we have that there exist $\omega_0\in\Omega$ and $\epsilon_0>0$ such that for any $0<\epsilon<\epsilon_0$, there exist infinitely many $n\in \mathbb N$ and corresponding $5\epsilon$-separated set in $M_{\omega_0}$ with respect to the Bowen metric $d_{M\times \Omega,n}^{\phi}$, whose cardinality is greater than $e^{n(\overline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\frac13\gamma)}$.

Firstly, we fix an such $\epsilon$ as  above. Without loss of generality, we assume that $\epsilon<\frac12\beta_0$, where $\beta_0$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing}. Letting $\beta=\frac13\epsilon$ and applying Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing}, we have that there exists $\alpha>0$ corresponding to $\beta$, which is taken to be smaller than $\beta$.  Then we fix a $\delta$ such that $\delta<\frac12\epsilon$ and
\begin{equation}\label{E:JumpControl}              
d_M(\pi_M\phi(x,\omega_1),\pi_M\phi(x,\omega_2))<\frac16 \alpha,\ \forall x\in M\text{ and }d_\Omega(\omega_1,\omega_2)<\delta.
\end{equation}
Let $\{U_0,U_1,\cdot,U_p\}$ be a collection of  $\frac13\alpha$-balls in $M$ such that $M=\cup_{i=1}^pU_i$. By Condition H2), there exists $N_1\in \mathbb N$ such that the following holds
$$\pi_M\phi^n(U_i,\omega)\cap U_j\neq \emptyset,\ \forall i,j\in \{0,1,\cdots,p\},\ n\ge N_1.$$
Now we fix an $N_2>> N_1$ such that there exists a $5\epsilon$-separated set in $M_{\omega_0}$ with respect to the Bowen metric $d_{M\times \Omega,N_2}^{\phi}$, whose cardinality is greater than $e^{N_2(\overline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\frac13\gamma)}$.  By the continuity of $\phi$, one can easily obtain the following technical lemma:
\begin{lem}\label{L:SeparatedSetFiber}                    
There exist a nonempty open subset $O\subset \Omega$ and  $k$ points $y_i:\in M,1\le i\le k$ with $$k\ge  e^{n(\overline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\frac13\gamma)}$$  such that for any $\omega\in O$, $\{(y_i,\omega)\}_{1\le i\le k}$ is a $3\epsilon$-separated set with respect to $d^{\phi}_{M\times \Omega,N_2}$.
\end{lem}
Actually, $O$ can be taken to be a small open neighborhood of $\omega_0$. For the sake  of convenience and without loss of generality, we assume that the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item[a1)] $O$ is in a  $\frac12\delta$-ball with respect to $d^{\theta}_{\Omega,N_2}$, where $\delta$ is as in (\ref{E:JumpControl});
\item[a2)] $\frac{\log k}{N_2}> \overline h(M\times \Omega|\Omega)-\frac23\gamma$;
\item[a3)] $\{y_i\}_{1\le i\le k}\subset U_0$ (Note that  $M$ is compact).
\end{itemize}

                                                            

Let $N=N_2+N_1$. Note that both $\Omega_1:=\bigcup_{i\in\mathbb Z}\theta^{iN}(O)$ and $\Omega_2:=\Omega\setminus \Omega_1$ are $\theta^N$-invariant sets since $\theta$ is invertible. Clearly, $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$ are both measurable ( actually $\Omega_1$ is open and $\Omega_2$ is closed). We will deal with $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$ separately.

Following exactly the same procedure as the proof of Lemma \ref{L:Horseshoe}, we can construct a  finite Borel measurable partition of $\Omega$, which is denoted by $\xi:=\{\Omega'_t, t\in T\}$,  Borel measurable simple functions $\{g^{0,0},g^{i,0},\ 1\le i\le p\}$, and a finite set $\{\omega_t\in \Omega'_t,t\in T\}$ satisfying the following properties:
\begin{itemize}
\item[b1)] For any $\omega,\omega'$ fall in an element of $\xi$, the following holds
$$d_\Omega(\theta^{ n}\omega,\theta^{ n}\omega')<\delta,\ \forall 0\le n\le N-1,$$
where $\delta$ satisfies (\ref{E:JumpControl});
\item[b2)] For $1\le i\le p$, $g^{i,0}=\sum_{t\in T}g^{i,0}_t\chi_{\Omega'_t}$, where
$$g^{i,0}_t\in U_i\text{ and }\pi_M\phi^{N_1}(g^{i,0}_t,\omega_t)\in U_0;$$
\item[b3)] $g^{0,0}=\sum_{t\in T}g^{0,0}_t\chi_{\Omega'_t}$, where
$$g^{0,0}_t\in U_0\text{ and } \pi_M\phi^{N}(g^{0,0}_t,\omega_t)\in U_0 \text{ for some }\omega_t\in \Omega'_t.$$
\end{itemize}
For each $i\in[1,k]\cap \mathbb N$,  there exists a finite Borel partition of $O$, which is denoted by $\eta_i:=\left\{O^i_q|q\in\{0,1,\cdots, p\}\right\}$, such that the following holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item[c1)]
$\pi_M\phi^{N_2}(\{y_{i}\}\times O^i_{q})\subset U_q$, where $\{y_i\}_{1\le i\le k}$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:SeparatedSetFiber}.
\end{itemize}
                                                                                                                                                                                                              

 Now, we are ready to construct the full random horseshoe by constructing proper pseudo orbits.

\noindent
{\bf \em  Step 1.} For each $\omega\in \Omega_1=\bigcup_{i\in\mathbb Z}\theta^{iN}(O)$, we first collect all the hitting time of orbit $\{\theta^{iN}\omega\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ with set $O$, which is denoted by $\{n_i(\omega)\}_{i\in I(\omega)}\subset \mathbb Z\cup\{\pm \infty\}$. We arrange $I(\omega)$ and $n_i(\omega)$ in the following way:


 \noindent
 {\em Case (1.1).} $n_i(\omega)$ has the same sign as $i$, and for any $i,j\in I (\omega)$,
 $$i< j\text{ if and only if  }n_i(\omega)< n_j(\omega) ;$$

  \noindent
 {\em Case (1.2).} For the positive part of $I(\omega)$, if $\{\theta^{iN}\omega\}_{i\in\mathbb N}$ hits $O$ infinitely many times, let
 $$I(\omega)\cap \mathbb N=\mathbb N;$$
 otherwise, let
 $$I(\omega)\cap \mathbb N=\{1,2,\cdots, m^+(\omega)\}\text{ and }n_{m^+(\omega)+1}=+\infty,$$
 where $m^+(\omega)$ is the number of times  $\{\theta^{iN}\omega\}_{i\in\mathbb N}$ hits $O$;

  \noindent
 {\em Case (1.3).} Similarly, for the negative part of $I(\omega)$,  if $\{\theta^{-iN}\omega\}_{i\in\mathbb N}$ hits $O$ infinitely many times, let $$I(\omega)\cap -\mathbb N=-\mathbb N;$$
 otherwise, let
 $$I(\omega)\cap -\mathbb N=\{-1,-2,\cdots, -m^-(\omega)\}\text{ and }n_{m^-(\omega)-1}=-\infty,$$ where
 $m^-(\omega)$ is the number of how many times  $\{\theta^{-iN}\omega\}_{i\in\mathbb N}$ hitting $O$;

  \noindent
 {\em Case (1.4).} If $\omega\in \theta^{-N_1}O$, put $0$ in $I(\omega)$ and let $n_0(\omega)=0$; otherwise, $0\notin I(\omega)$.\\



  We remark here that $I(\omega)$ is always non-empty for $\omega\in \Omega_1$, however, each of $I(\omega)\cap \mathbb N$, $I(\omega)\cap \{0\}$, and $I(\omega)\cap -\mathbb N$ could be an empty set.
 \medskip

 \noindent
 {\bf \em Step 2.} For a given $\omega\in\Omega_1$ and $\hat a=(a_n)\in \mathcal S^k$, we define a pseudo orbit as in the following:


  \noindent
 {\em Case 1.} For $n=n_i(\omega)$, $i\in I(\omega)$, suppose that
 $$\theta^{nN}\omega\in O^{a_n}_q \text{ and } \theta^{nN+N_2}\omega\in \Omega'_{t_1},$$
  then define
 \begin{equation}\label{E:POCase1}          
 y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+j)=
 \begin{cases}
 \pi_M\phi^{j}(y_{a_n},\theta^{nN}\omega),&0\le j\le N_2-1\\
 \pi_M\phi^{j-N_2}(g^{q,0}(\theta^{nN+N_2}\omega),\omega_{t_1}),&N_2\le j\le N-1\\
 \end{cases}.
 \end{equation}


  \noindent
 {\it Case 2.} For $n\notin\{n_i(\omega)\}_{i\in I(\omega)}$, suppose that $\theta^{nN}\omega\in \Omega'_{t_2}$,
 then define
 \begin{equation}\label{E:POCase2}          
 y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+j)=\pi_M\phi^j(g^{0,0}(\theta^{nN}\omega),\omega_{t_2}),\ 0\le j\le N-1.
 \end{equation}




 For Case 1., note that $\{(y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+j),\theta^{nN+j}\omega\}_{0\le j\le N_2-1}$ is a true orbit, and $\theta^{nN}\in O^{a_n}_q$, therefore
 $$\pi_M\phi(y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+N_2-1),\theta^{nN+N_2-1}\omega),\ y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+N_2)\in U_q,$$
 thus
 $$d_M\left(\pi_M\phi(y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+N_2-1),\theta^{nN+N_2-1}\omega),\ y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+N_2)\right)\le \frac23\alpha.$$

                            
                
                                                                                               
                                                                                                                          
                                                                               
                             
              




 By b1) and (\ref{E:JumpControl}), we have that for $N_2\le j\le N-1$,
 \begin{align*}
 &d_M\left(\pi_M\phi\left( y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+j),\theta^{nN+j}\omega\right), y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+j+1)\right)\\
 =&d_M\left(\pi_M\phi\left(\pi_M\phi^j(g^{q,0}(\theta^{nN+N_2}\omega),\omega_{t_1}),\theta^{nN+N_2+j}\omega\right), \pi_M\phi^{j+1}(g^{q,0}(\theta^{nN+N_2}\omega),\omega_{t_1})\right)\\
 \le &\frac16\alpha,
 \end{align*}
 which implies that $\{(y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+j),\theta^{nN+j}\omega\}_{N_2\le j\le N-1}$ is a segment of an $(\omega,\frac16\alpha)$-pseudo orbit.
 Hence $\{(y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+j),\theta^{nN_j}\omega\}_{0\le j\le N-1}$ is a segment of an $(\omega,\frac23\alpha)$-pseudo orbit with length $N$. \\

 For Case 2., by b3), (\ref{E:JumpControl}), and using the same argument as for $N_2\le j\le N-1$ in Case 1., we have that
$\{(y'_{\hat a,\omega}(nN+j),\theta^{nN_j}\omega\}_{0\le j\le N-1}$ is a segment of an $(\omega,\frac16\alpha)$-pseudo orbit with length $N$.

Also note that, all the segments of $(\omega,\alpha)$-pseudo orbit defined in both Case 1. and Case 2. start and end in $U_0$ which has diameter $\frac23\alpha$. Hence, the pseudo orbit $\{(y'_{\hat a,\omega}(j),\theta^{j}\omega\}_{j\in \mathbb Z}$ is an $(\omega,\frac23\alpha)$-pseudo orbit.

It is clear that $\{(y'_{\hat a,\omega}(j),\theta^{j}\omega\}_{j\in \mathbb Z},\ \omega\in\Omega$ induces an $\alpha$-pseudo orbit of $\tilde\phi$ by letting
$$g'_{\hat a,j}(\omega)=y'_{\hat a,\omega}(j),\ j\in \mathbb Z,\ \omega\in\Omega_1.$$
The Borel measurability of each $g'_{\hat a,j}$ follows from (\ref{E:POCase1}) and (\ref{E:POCase2}) immediately, since each $g'_{\hat a,j}$ is either a simple function or an image of a simple function under iterations of $\phi$ or $\phi^{-1}$. Therefore, by applying Theorem \ref{L:LShad} for $\tilde\phi|_{L^\infty(\Omega_1)}$, we have that   there exists a unique true orbit of $\tilde\phi|_{L^\infty(\Omega_1)}$, $\{(\tilde\phi|_{L^\infty(\Omega_1)})^n(g_{\hat a})\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}$, which is $\beta$-shadowing $\{g'_{\hat a,j}\}_{j\in \mathbb Z}$.


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                               
 
                                                                                                                          
 
                                                   
                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                
 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                   

         
                                                                                                              
                
                               
                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                              
              
 
 
 
                                         
                                                                                         
                                                                                                                   

\medskip

Now we define the desired horseshoe map by the letting
$$\Psi(\hat a)|_{\Omega_1}=g_{\hat a},\ \forall \hat a\in \mathcal S_k.$$
The continuity of $\Psi|_{\Omega_1}$ follows from  Lemma \ref{L:ContinousShadowing} straightforwardly. The next, we prove that   Condition i) of Definition \ref{D:RandomHorseshoe} for $\Psi|_{\Omega_1}$ holds.

For $\hat a'\neq\hat a'' (\in \mathcal S_k)$, let $s=\min\left\{|n|\big |\ a'_n\neq a''_n\right\}$ and $r$  be such that $|r|=s$ and $a'_r\neq a''_r$ .
By the choice of $O,y_i,U_i,\epsilon,\alpha,\beta$ at the beginning of this section,  we have that
 $$d^\phi_{M\times \Omega,N_1}\left(\phi^{rN}(\Psi(\hat a_1)(\omega),\omega),\phi^{rN}(\Psi(\hat a_2)(\omega),\omega)\right)>\epsilon,\ \forall \omega\in \theta^{-rN}(O),$$
 where $d^\phi_{M\times \Omega,N_1}$ is the Bowen metric.
 Note that there is a constant $L>1$ such that for any $\omega\in\Omega$ and $x,y\in M$ with $d(x,y)>0$, we have
 $$d(\phi^{\pm1}(x,\omega),\phi^{\pm1}(y,\omega))\le Ld_M(x,y).$$
 Therefore, for any $\omega$ from the non-empty open set $\theta^{-rN}(O)$, the following holds,
 \begin{align*}
& d_M\left(\pi_M\phi^{rN}\left(\Psi(\hat a_1)(\omega),\omega\right),\pi_M\phi^{rN}\left(\Psi(\hat a_2)(\omega),\omega\right)\right)\\
=&d\left(\phi^{rN}\left(\Psi(\hat a_1)(\omega),\omega\right),\phi^{rN}\left(\Psi(\hat a_2)(\omega),\omega\right)\right)\\
\ge& L^{-N_1}d^\phi_{M\times \Omega,N_1}\left(\phi^{rN}(\Psi(\hat a_1)(\omega),\omega),\phi^{rN}(\Psi(\hat a_2)(\omega),\omega)\right)\\
>& \epsilon L^{-N},
 \end{align*}
 which implies Condition i) of  Definition \ref{D:RandomHorseshoe} by taking $\Delta=  \epsilon L^{-N}$.
  The continuity of $\Psi^{-1}$ follows from the same argument as (\ref{E:PsiInverseContinuity}).

 \noindent {\bf \em  Final Step.} To complete the proof, we  need to address the following  issues:

 Firstly, Condition ii) in Definition \ref{D:RandomHorseshoe} for $\Psi|_{\Omega_1}$ simply follows from the uniqueness of $g_{\hat a}$ and the same argument used in the proof of Lemma \ref{L:Horseshoe}.

 Secondly,  we need to extend the definition of $g_{\hat a}$ properly to the whole $\Omega$. This can be done by Theorem \ref{T:TheoryAnosovMix}. Since $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2=\Omega\setminus \Omega_2$ are both $\theta^N$-invariant, we can view $\Omega_2$ independently, and give up to capture entropy from the system $\phi^N|_{\Omega_2}$ (as the entropy captured from $\phi^N|_{\Omega_1}$ is already enough). Theorem \ref{T:TheoryAnosovMix} implies that for large $N$, there exists a Borel function $g:\Omega_2\to M$ such that
 $$\phi^N|_{\Omega_2}(graph(g))=graph(g).$$
 We simply extend $g_{\hat a}$ to $\tilde g_{\hat a}$ by letting
 $$\tilde g_{\hat a}|_{\Omega_1}=g_{\hat a}\text{ and }\tilde g_{\hat a}|_{\Omega_2}=g.$$
 It is not hard to see that such an extension is harmless for  Conditions i) and ii) of Definition \ref{D:RandomHorseshoe}. So the map $\Psi:\mathcal S_k\to L^\infty$ which takes $\hat a$ to $\tilde g_{\hat a}$ gives a full random horseshoe.

 Finally, as we required at the beginning of this section that $N_2>>N_1$, a2) yields
 $$\frac{\log k}N=\frac{\log k}{N_2+2N_1}>\frac{\log k}{N_2}-\frac13\gamma>\overline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)-\gamma.$$
                                                                                                       
This completes  the proof of theorem.

label: E:MeasAppr
title: Proof
body_md:
We first fix a $\theta$-invariant probability measure $\mathbb P$ on $\Omega$. We will show that for any $\mu\in \mathcal I_{\mathbb P}(M\times\Omega)$, there is a sequence of periodic measures $\{\mu_i\}_{i=1,2,\cdots}$ such that for any continuous real function $h$ defined on $M\times\Omega$ the following holds
$$\int h d\mu=\lim_{i\to\infty} \int hd\mu_i.$$
Since $C(M\times\Omega)$, the space of continuous real functions defined on a compact set, is separable, it suffices to show that for any $\mu\in \mathcal I_{\mathbb P}(M\times\Omega)$, $\epsilon>0$ and $h\in C(M\times \Omega)$, there is a periodic measure $\mu_{\epsilon}^h$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{E:MeasAppr}           
\left|\int hd\mu-\int hd\mu_{\epsilon}^h\right|<\epsilon.
\end{equation}
To the end, based on the above assertion, it is not hard to see that $\{\mu_{\frac1n}^{h_m}\}_{n,m\in \mathbb N}$ forms an countable dense subset of $\mathcal I_{\mathbb P}(M\times\Omega)$, where $\{h_m\}_{m\in\mathbb N}$ is a dense subset of $C(M\times\Omega)$.

Fixing $\mu\in \mathcal I_{\mathbb P}(M\times\Omega)$, $\epsilon>0$ and $h\in C(M\times \Omega)$, we now construct $\mu_{\epsilon}^h$.

Since $h$ is uniformly continuous on $M\times \Omega$ by the compactness of $M\times\Omega$,
there exists $\delta_1>0$ such that the following holds
\begin{equation}\label{E:Delta1AndEpsilon}                    
|h(x_1,\omega)-h(x_2,\omega)|<\frac1{10}\epsilon,\text{ provided }d_M(x_1,x_2)<\delta_1.
\end{equation}

By Lemma \ref{L:LShad}, there exists $\delta_2>0$ such that any $\delta_2$-pseudo orbit  can be $\frac13\delta_1$-shadowed by a unique true orbit of $\tilde\phi$.
By Lemma \ref{L:JoinSegments}, there exists an $N_1\in \mathbb N$ such that for any $g_1,g_2\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$,  there exists a $g_3\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{E:JoinGraph}            
\max\left\{d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(g_3,g_1),d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(\tilde\phi^{N_1}(g_3),g_2)\right\}<\frac13\delta_2.
\end{equation}
For $m\in\mathbb N$ and $s>0$, let $$A_{m,s}^h:=\left\{(x,\omega)\in M\times\Omega\Big|\ \left|\int hd\mu-\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}h\left(\phi^i(x,\omega)\right)\right|<s,\ \forall n\ge m\right\}.$$
It is not hard to see that $A_{m,s}^h$ is a $G_{\delta}$-set by the continuity of $h$ and $\phi$, and $\lim_{m\to\infty}\mu(A_{m,s}^h)=1$ by the Birkhoff ergodic theorem. Now fix an $N_2\in\mathbb N$ such that the following holds
\begin{equation}\label{E:LargePeriod}              
\mathbb P \left(\pi_\Omega\left(A_{N_2,\frac15\epsilon}^h\right)\right)>1-\frac1{4M}\epsilon\text{ and }\frac{N_1}{N_2}<\frac1{10M}\epsilon,
\end{equation}
where $M=\sup_{M\times\Omega}|h|$.

Note that $\mu$ is regular. Then, there exists a compact set $K\subset A_{N_2,\frac15\epsilon}^h$ such that
$$\mathbb P \left(\pi_\Omega\left(K\right)\right)>1-\frac14\epsilon.$$
Applying Theorem \ref{T:BMST}, we have that there is a Borel map $g:\Omega\to M$ such that the following holds
$$g(\omega)\in K,\ \forall x\in \pi_\Omega\left(K\right).$$

Let $N=N_1+N_2$. By (\ref{E:JoinGraph}), we have that there exists an $\delta_2$-pseudo orbit $\{(g_n'\}_{n\in \mathbb Z}$ satisfying the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item[a)] $g'_{lN}=g,\ \forall l\in \mathbb Z$;
\item[b)] $g'_{lN+k}=\tilde\phi^{k}(g),\ \forall 0\le k\le N_2-1$.
 \end{itemize}
Therefore, by Lemma \ref{L:LShad}, there exists a true orbit $\{\tilde\phi^n(\tilde g_0)\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ of $\tilde\phi$,  which is $\frac13\delta_1$-shadowing $\{g_n'\}_{n\in \mathbb Z}$.  By the uniqueness of the shadowing orbit, it is not hard to see that $\tilde g_0$ is a random periodic point with period $N$.

Next, we show that the periodic measure induced by $graph(\tilde g_0)$
$$\mu_\epsilon^h:=\frac1N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\mu_{\tilde g_i},\text{ provided }graph(\tilde g_i)=\phi^i(graph(\tilde g_0)),\ 0\le i\le N-1,$$
satisfies (\ref{E:MeasAppr}).

Note that $\mathbb P$ can be decomposed into the following form
$$\mathbb P=\sum_{i\in I} a_i\nu_i,$$
where $card(I)\le N$, $a_i>0$, $\sum_{i\in I}a_i=1$, and $\nu_i$ is $\theta^N$-ergodic.

By Birkhoff ergodic theorem, there exists an $\phi$-invariant Borel function $\tilde h:M\times \Omega$ such that
$$\tilde h(x,\omega)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}h\left(\phi^i(x,\omega)\right),\ \mu_\epsilon^h-a.e.,$$
and
$$\int \tilde hd\mu_\epsilon^h=\int hd\mu_\epsilon^h.$$
Suppose that $(\tilde g_0(\omega),\omega)$ is a regular point of $\mu_\epsilon^h$ while $\omega$ is a regular point of $\nu_i$ for some $i\in I$, which can be done because the set of regular points of an invariant measure occupies full probability. Denote that
$$\mathcal K(n):=card\left(\left\{k|\ 0\le k\le n-1,\theta^{kN}\in \pi_\Omega(K)\right\}\right).$$ Then we have that,
\begin{align*}
&\left|\tilde h(\tilde g_0(\omega),\omega)-\int hd\mu\right|\\
=&\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac1{nN}\sum_{i=0}^{nN-1}h\left(\phi^i(\tilde g_0(\omega),\omega)\right)-\int hd\mu\right|\\
\le&\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1{nN}\Bigg\{\sum_{0\le k\le n-1,\theta^{kN}\in \pi_\Omega(K)}\left|\sum_{i=kN}^{(k+1)N-1}h\left(\phi^i(\tilde g_0(\omega),\omega)\right)-N\int hd\mu\right|\\
&\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad+\sum_{0\le k\le n-1,\theta^{kN}\notin \pi_\Omega(K)}\left|\sum_{i=kN}^{(k+1)N-1}h\left(\phi^i(\tilde g_0(\omega),\omega)\right)-N\int hd\mu\right|\Bigg\}\\
\le&\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1{nN}\Bigg\{\sum_{0\le k\le n-1,\theta^{kN}\in \pi_\Omega(K)}\sum_{i=kN}^{(k+1)N-1}\left|h\left(\phi^i(\tilde g_0(\omega),\omega)\right)-h\left(\phi^{i-kN}( g(\theta^{kN}\omega),\theta^{kN}\omega)\right)\right|\\
&\quad\quad+\sum_{0\le k\le n-1,\theta^{kN}\in \pi_\Omega(K)}\left[\left|\sum_{i=kN}^{kN+N_2-1}h\left(\phi^{i-kN}( g(\theta^{kN}\omega),\theta^{kN}\omega)\right)-N_2\int hd\mu\right|+2N_1M\right]\\
&\quad\quad+\sum_{0\le k\le n-1,\theta^{kN}\notin \pi_\Omega(K)}2NM\Bigg\}\\
\le &\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1{nN}\left\{\mathcal K(n)\left(\frac1{10}N\epsilon+\frac15N_2\epsilon+2N_1M\right)+2NM(n-\mathcal K(n))\right\}\\
\le&\frac12\nu_i(K)\epsilon+2M(1-\nu_i(\pi_\Omega (K)))\\
\le& \frac12\epsilon+2M(1-\nu_i(\pi_\Omega(K))).
\end{align*}
In the above argument, condition b), (\ref{E:Delta1AndEpsilon}) and  $K\subset A_{N_2,\frac15\epsilon}^h$ are used.

Therefore, as $\tilde h$ being $\phi$-invariant, we have that
\begin{align*}
&\left|\int \tilde hd\mu_\epsilon^h-\int h d\mu\right|=\left|\int \tilde hd\mu_{\tilde g_0}-\int h d\mu\right|\\
\le&\int\left|\tilde h(\tilde g_0(\omega),\omega)-\int hd\mu\right|d\mu_{\tilde g_0}=\int\left|\tilde h(\tilde g_0(\omega),\omega)-\int hd\mu\right|d\mathbb P\\
=&\sum_{i\in I}a_i\int\left|\tilde h(\tilde g_0(\omega),\omega)-\int hd\mu\right|d\nu_i\le\sum_{i\in I}a_i\left(\frac12\epsilon+2M(1-\nu_i(\pi_\Omega(K)))\right)\\
=&\frac12\epsilon+2M(1-\mathbb P(\pi_\Omega(K)))<\epsilon,
\end{align*}
which completes the proof. \qed
