label: E:EstOnOrbit
title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{L:InvMani}, \ref{L:LocCoor}, and P2) in the proof of Lemma \ref{L:ClosingLemma}, for a fixed positive number $\lambda\in(0,\lambda_0)$, there exist $\epsilon>0$, $\delta\in(0,\epsilon)$, $L>1$ such that for any $x,y\in M$ with $d_M(x,y)<\delta$, the following hold
\begin{align*}
& [x,y]_\omega=:W^s_{\epsilon}(x,\omega)\cap W^u_{\epsilon}(y,\omega),\text{ which is continuous on }x,y\text{ and }\omega,\\
&\max\left\{d_M(x,[x,y]_\omega),d_M(y,[x,y]_\omega)\right\}\le Ld_M(x,y),\\
&d_M(\pi_M\phi^n(x,\omega),\pi_M\phi^n(y,\omega))\le e^{-n\lambda}d_M(x,y)\text{ for }(y,\omega)\in W^s_{\epsilon}(x,\omega),\ n\ge 0,\\
&d_M(\pi_M\phi^{-n}(x,\omega),\pi_M\phi^{-n}(y,\omega))\le e^{-n\lambda}d_M(x,y)\text{ for }(y,\omega)\in W^u_{\epsilon}(x,\omega),\ n\ge 0.
\end{align*}
For $(g,n)\in \mathcal G$ and $h\in B_n(g,\epsilon)$, we have that for any $\omega\in\Omega$ and $0\le i\le n-1$
\begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:EstOnOrbit}             
&d_M(\pi_M\phi^i(g(\omega),\omega),\pi_M\phi^i(h(\omega),\omega)))\\
\le &d_M\left(\pi_M\phi^i(g(\omega),\omega),\left[\pi_M\phi^i(g(\omega),\omega),\pi_M\phi^i(h(\omega),\omega))\right]_{\theta^i\omega}\right)\\
&+d_M\left(\pi_M\phi^i(h(\omega),\omega),\left[\pi_M\phi^i(g(\omega),\omega),\pi_M\phi^i(h(\omega),\omega))\right]_{\theta^i\omega}\right)\\
\le &e^{-i\lambda}d_M\left(g(\omega),\left[g(\omega),h(\omega)\right]_{\omega}\right)\\
&+e^{-(n-1-i)\lambda}d_M\left(\pi_M\phi^{n-1}(h(\omega),\omega),\left[\pi_M\phi^{n-1}(g(\omega),\omega),\pi_M\phi^{n-1}(h(\omega),\omega))\right]_{\theta^{n-1}\omega}\right)\\
\le&2Le^{-i\lambda}d_M(g(\omega),h(\omega))+2Le^{-(n-1-i)\lambda}d_M(\pi_M\phi^{n-1}(g(\omega),\omega),\pi_M\phi^{n-1}(h(\omega),\omega))\\
\le&4Le^{-\min\{i,n-1-i\}\lambda}\epsilon.
\end{split}
\end{align}
                                                                                          
                                                            
                                                                                                    


Then
\begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:VarEstBP}           
&\sup_{\mathbb P}|S_n(\psi(g(\omega),\omega))-S_n(\psi(h(\omega),\omega))|\\
\le &\sup_{\mathbb P}\|\psi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}(4L\epsilon)^\alpha\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}e^{-\min\{i,n-1-i\}\alpha\lambda}\\<&\frac{2 \sup_{\mathbb P}\|\psi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}(4L\epsilon)^\alpha}{1-e^{-\alpha\lambda}},
\end{split}
\end{align}
which is independent on $n$, $g$ and $h$.

For the average Bowen property, we need only to replace the $\sup_{\mathbb P}$ in (\ref{E:VarEstBP}) by integration on $\Omega$ with respect to $\mathbb P$ and obtain the following
\begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:VarEstABP}            
&\int_{\Omega}|S_n(\psi(g(\omega),\omega))-S_n(\psi(h(\omega),\omega))|d\mathbb P\\
\le&\int_{\Omega}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left|\psi\left(\phi^i(g(\omega),\omega)\right)-\psi\left(\phi^i(h(\omega),\omega)\right)\right|\\
\le &\int_{\Omega}(4L\epsilon)^\alpha\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\|\psi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_{\theta^i\omega})}e^{-\min\{i,n-1-i\}\alpha\lambda}d\mathbb P\\
<&\frac{2(4L\epsilon)^\alpha}{1-e^{-\alpha\lambda}}\int_{\Omega} \|\psi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}d\mathbb P,
\end{split}
\end{align}
which is independent on $n$, $g$ and $h$.
This completes the proof of this lemma.

label: L:TransitiveOnC(Ome,M)
title: Proof
body_md:
At first, we prove a the following technical lemma:
\begin{lem}\label{L:TransitiveOnC(Ome,M)}                       
There exists an orbit of $\tilde\phi$, whose closure contains $C(\Omega,M)$.
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
Note that $C(\Omega,M)$ is separable since $M$ and $\Omega$ are compact. Let $\{g_i\}_{i=1,2,\cdots}\subset C(\Omega,M)$ be a countable dense set of $C(\Omega,M)$. Denote $U_{ij}$ the $\frac1j$-ball centered at $g_i$ in $C(\Omega,M)$.
                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                       
We relabel the countable set $\left\{U_{i,j}\right\}_{i,j=1,2,\cdots}$ and denote the relabeled set by $\{V_k\}_{k=1,2\cdots}$ which satisfies the following rule:
$$\text{ for }V_{k_1}=U_{i_1j_1}, V_{k_2}=U_{i_2j_2},\ k_1\le k_2\text{ iff } i_1+j_1\le i_2+j_2\text{ or } i_1+j_1= i_2+j_2,i_1\le i_2.$$
We also define a function $l:\mathbb N\to \mathbb N$ by letting $l(k)=i$ when $V_k=U_{ij}$.\\

Let $\alpha$ be as in Lemma \ref{L:LShad} for a fixed $\beta\in(0,\beta_0)$.
By Lemma \ref{L:JoinSegments}, for any $n_k,n_{k+1}\in\mathbb N$, there exist $\{g'_k\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)\}_{k=1,2,\cdots}$ and $m\in\mathbb N$ such that
$$\max\left\{d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}\left(\tilde\phi^{n_k}g_{l(k)},g'_k\right),\ d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}\left(\tilde\phi^{m}g'_k,\tilde\phi^{-n_{k+1}}g_{l(k+1)}\right)\right\}<\alpha.$$
Therefore, we have that $\mathcal G_{0},\mathcal G_1,\mathcal G_2,\cdots$ form an $\alpha$-pseudo orbit of $\tilde\phi$, where we let
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal G_{0}&=\{\tilde\phi^{-n}g_{l(1)}\}_{n\ge 1}\\
\mathcal G_k&=\left\{g_{l(k)},\cdots,\tilde\phi^{n_k-1}g_{l(k)},g'_k,\cdots,\tilde\phi^{m-1}g'_k,\tilde \phi^{-n_{k+1}}g_{l(k+1)},\cdots, \tilde\phi^{-1}g_{l(k+1)}\right\},\ k\in \mathbb N.
\end{align*}
  Thus,  Lemma \ref{L:LShad} implies that there exists a $g\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ such that
$$d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}\left(\tilde\phi^{\pm(n_1-1)}g,\tilde\phi^{\pm(n_1-1)}g_{l(1)}\right)<\beta,$$
 and
 $$d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}\left(\tilde\phi^{\pm (n_{k+1}-1)}\left(\tilde\phi^{\sum_{i=1}^k(n_i+n_{i+1}+m)}g\right),\tilde\phi^{\pm n_{k+1}-1}g_{l(k+1)}\right)<\beta,\ \forall k\ge 1.$$
By applying Lemma \ref{L:ContinousShadowing} and choosing $n_k$ large enough for each $k\ge 1$, we have the following:
\begin{equation}\label{E:ADenseOrbit}              
g\subset V_1\text{ and }\tilde\phi^{\sum_{i=1}^k(n_i+n_{i+1}+m)}g\subset V_{k+1},\ \forall k\ge 1,
\end{equation}
which implies that
\begin{equation}\label{E:ADenseOrbit1}               
C(\Omega,M)\subset \text{ closure of }\{\tilde \phi^n(g)\}_{n\ge 0} \text{ in }L^\infty(\Omega, M).
\end{equation}
\end{proof}
\medskip

Now we define a functional on $\{\tilde \phi^n(g)\}_{n\ge 0}$ by the following
\begin{equation}\label{E:PsiOnOrb}           
\hat \Psi'(\tilde \phi^n(g))=\sum_{i=0}^n\tilde\Phi(\tilde \phi^i(g))
\end{equation}

From Lemma \ref{L:MixToSpecification} and the second part of Lemma \ref{L:BowenPro}, it follows  that $\hat \Psi ''$ is bounded on $\{\tilde \phi^n(g)\}_{n\ge 0}$. In fact, there exist $N\in\mathbb N$ and $\epsilon\in (0,\epsilon_0)$ (where $\epsilon_0$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:BowenPro}) such that for any $n\in \mathbb N$, there exists a periodic point $h\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ such tha the following hold:
$$\tilde \phi^{n+N}(h)=h\text{ and }d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(\tilde \phi^i(g),\tilde \phi^i(h))\le \epsilon,\ i=0,1,\cdots, n.$$
Therefore,  by (\ref{E:VarEstABP}) we have that
\begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:PsiSupNormEst}                
\left|\hat \Psi'(\tilde \phi^n(g))\right|&\le \sum_{i=n+1}^{n+N-1}\left|\tilde \Phi(\tilde\phi^i(h))\right|+\sum_{i=0}^n\left|\tilde\Phi(\tilde\phi^i(h))-\tilde\Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g))\right|\\
&\le \left(N+\frac{2(4L\epsilon)^\alpha}{1-e^{-\alpha\lambda}}\right)\int_{\Omega} \|\Phi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}d\mathbb P,
\end{split}
\end{align}
which is independent on $n$.


Let $\alpha_0>0$ and $C$ be the constants as in the second part of Lemma \ref{L:LShad}. We have that for any $\alpha\in(0,\alpha_0)$ each $\alpha$-pseudo orbit of $\tilde\phi$ can be $C\alpha$-shadowed. Without loss of generality, we assume that $C\alpha_0<\epsilon_0$, where $\epsilon_0$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:BowenPro}. Suppose that for $n,k\in\mathbb N$ $d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(\tilde \phi^{n+k}(g),\tilde \phi^{n}(g))<\alpha_0$. By applying Lemma \ref{L:LShad}, there exists a random periodic point $g_0\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ such that the following holds
$$\tilde \phi^k(g_0)=g_0\text{ and }d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(\tilde \phi^i(g_0),\tilde\phi^{n+i}(g))<(C+1)d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(\tilde \phi^{n+k}(g),\tilde \phi^{n}(g)), i=0,1,\cdots, k.$$
Therefore, we obtain that
\begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:PsiHolderNormEst}                   
&\left|\hat\Psi'(\tilde \phi^{n+k}(g))-\hat\Psi'(\tilde \phi^{n}(g))\right|\\
=&\left|\sum_{i=n+1}^{n+k}\tilde \Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g))-\sum_{i=1}^{k}\tilde \Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g_0))\right|\ \left(\text{by }(\ref{E:PeriodicNull})\sum_{i=1}^{k}\tilde \Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g_0))=0\right)\\
\le&\sum_{i=1}^{k}\left|\tilde \Phi(\tilde\phi^{n+i}(g))-\tilde\Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g_0))\right|\\
\le&C_1\left(d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}(\tilde \phi^{n+k}(g),\tilde \phi^{n}(g))\right)^\alpha \ \left(\text{Applying }(\ref{E:VarEstABP})\right),
\end{split}
\end{align}
where $C_1=\frac{2\left(4L(C+1)\right)^\alpha}{1-e^{-\alpha\lambda}}\int_{\Omega}\|\Phi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}d\mathbb P$ and $L$ is as in (\ref{E:VarEstABP}).

 So far, we have shown that $\hat \Psi '$ is $\alpha$-H\"older continuous and bounded on $\{\tilde \phi^n(g)\}_{n\ge 0}$. As $\{\tilde \phi^n(g)\}_{n\ge 0}$ being dense in $C(\Omega,M)$, $\hat \Psi '$ defined by (\ref{E:PsiOnOrb}) has a unique $\alpha$-H\"older extension $\hat\Psi$ on $C(\Omega,M)$,  which completes the proof.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:PsiAbsCon}            
There exists $L'>0$ such that  for any given $\Phi\in L^1_{\mathbb P}(\Omega,C^{0,\alpha}(M))$ satisfying (\ref{E:PeriodicNull}) and the associated $\hat\Psi$ as in Lemma \ref{L:WLivThC}  the following holds
\begin{equation}\label{E:PsiAbsCon}            
\left|\hat \Psi(h_1)-\hat \Psi(h_2)\right|\le L'\overline\Phi\left(3\mathbb P\left(\Omega\setminus \Omega_{h_1,h_2,\rho}\right)\right)+L'\rho^\alpha\int_{\Omega}\|\Phi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}d\mathbb P,\ \forall h_1,h_2\in C(\Omega,M),
\end{equation}
where $$\Omega_{h_1,h_2,\rho}=\left\{\omega\in\Omega\big|\ d_M(h_1(\omega), h_2(\omega))< \rho\right\}$$ and $$\overline\Phi(s):=\sup_{A\subset \Omega:\mathbb P(A)\le s}\int_{A} \|\Phi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}d\mathbb P,\  s\in (0,1).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\hat \Psi'$ is bounded, it suffices to consider the case when $\rho$  and  $\mathbb P\left(\Omega\setminus \Omega_{h_1,h_2,\rho}\right)$ are small.

Let $g\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ be the point that the closure of whose orbit contains $C(\Omega,M)$, and $\alpha_0$ be as in the second part of Lemma \ref{L:LShad}, and  $\alpha_1\in (0,\frac16\alpha_0)$. By Lemma \ref{L:JoinSegments}, there exists an $N_1\in \mathbb N$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{E:N-connect}            
 \forall g_1,g_2\in L^\infty(\Omega, M),\ \exists g_3\in L^\infty(\Omega, M) \text{ s.t. }g_3\in B(g_1,\alpha_1)\text{ and }\tilde\phi^{N_1} (g_3)\in B(g_2,\alpha_1),
 \end{equation}
  where $B(h,r)$ is the $r$-ball centered at $h$ in $L^\infty(\Omega, M)$.

                                                                                                                                                                   
                                                
                                                                                                                                                       
                
                                                                                                                                                      

Given $\rho\in (0,\alpha_1)$ and $h_1,h_2\in C(\Omega,M)$, we denote $\Omega_1=\Omega\setminus \Omega_{h_1,h_2,\rho}$. For $\alpha_2\in(0,\frac12\rho)$, let $n,k\in\mathbb N$ be such that $\tilde \phi^n(g)\in B(h_1,\alpha_2)$ and $\tilde \phi^{n+k}(g)\in B(h_2,\alpha_2)$. Without loss of generality, we assume that $n,k>>N_1$. By the choice of $\alpha_1$ and $N_1$, there exists $h_3\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ satisfying the following
$$h_3\in B(\tilde \phi^{n+k-N_1}(g),\alpha_1)\text{ and }\tilde\phi^{N_1}(h_3)\in B(h_1,\alpha_1).$$
Define a periodic sequence $\{g_i\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}\subset L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ with period $k$ by the following:
\begin{equation}\label{E:PeriodicPartialConnect}                         
g_i=\begin{cases}
\tilde \phi^{i+n}(g), &\text{when }0\le i\le k-N_1-1\\
\tilde \phi^{i+N_1}(g)\chi_{\Omega\setminus \theta^{-N_1}\Omega_1}+h_3\chi_{ \theta^{-N_1}\Omega_1},&\text{when }i=k-N_1\\
\tilde\phi^{i-k+N_1}g_{k-N_1}, &\text{when }k-N_1+1\le i\le k-1\\
g_{i\mod k}&\text{otherwise}
\end{cases},
\end{equation}
where $\chi_{O}$ is the characteristic function of $O\subset \Omega$.
It is clear that
$$\tilde\phi(g_i)\in B(g_{i+1},\rho+2\alpha_1+2\alpha_2),\ \forall i\in\mathbb Z.$$
Thus, using $\alpha_1,\alpha_2, \rho\in(0,\frac16\alpha_0)$ and Lemma \ref{L:LShad}, we obtain that there exists a random periodic point $g'$ satisfying that
\begin{equation}\label{E:PeriodicShadowg'}                   
\tilde\phi^i(g')\in B(g_i,C(\rho+2\alpha_1+2\alpha_2)),\ i\in\mathbb Z,
\end{equation}
where $C$ is the one as in Lemma \ref{L:LShad}.

Note that for each $\omega\in \Omega\setminus \Omega'$ where $\Omega'= \Omega_1\cup \theta^{-k}\Omega_1\cup \theta^{-2k}\Omega_1$, we have that
$$
g_i(\theta^i\omega)=\begin{cases}
\tilde\phi^{n+i-k}(g)(\theta^i\omega)&k\le i\le 2k-1\\
\tilde\phi^{n+i}(g)(\theta^i\omega)&0\le i\le k-1\\
\tilde\phi^{n+k+i}(g)(\theta^i\omega)&-k\le i\le-1\\
\end{cases}.
$$
Thus, we have  a $(\rho+\alpha_1,\omega)$-pseudo orbit $\{(y_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in \mathbb Z}$ by letting
$$(y_i,\theta^i\omega)=
\begin{cases}
\phi^{i-2k+1}\left(g_{2k-1}(\theta^{2k-1}\omega),\theta^{2k-1}\omega\right)&i\ge 2k\\
\left(g_i(\theta^i\omega),\theta^i\omega\right)&-k\le i\le 2k-1\\
\phi^{i+k}\left(g_{-k}(\theta^{-k}\omega),\theta^{-k}\omega\right)&i\le -k-1\\
\end{cases}.$$
Here $\{(y_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ is a $(\rho+2\alpha_2,\omega)$-pseudo orbit because $\{\left(g_i(\theta^i\omega),\theta^i\omega\right)\}_{-k\le i\le 2k-1}$ is a segment of a $(\rho+2\alpha_2,\omega)$-pseudo orbit. By Lemma \ref{L:ClosingLemma} and the choice of $\alpha_2$ and $\rho$, we have that there exists a true orbit $\{\phi^i(y',\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ which is $(C(\rho+2\alpha_2),\omega)$-shadowing $\{(y_i,\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$. Recall that $\{\phi^i(g'(\omega),\omega)\}_{-k\le i\le 2k}$ is $(C(\rho+2\alpha_1+2\alpha_2),\omega)$-shadowing $\{\left(g_i(\theta^i\omega),\theta^i\omega\right)\}_{-k\le i\le 2k-1}$, which means that
$$\max_{-k\le i\le 2k-1}d_M\left(\pi_M\phi^i(g'(\omega),\omega),\pi_M\phi^i(y',\omega)\right)\le C(2\alpha_1+4\alpha_2+2\rho),\ \forall \omega\in\Omega\setminus \Omega'.$$
Note that $k$ can be chosen arbitrarily large. Hence Lemma \ref{L:ContinousShadowing} implies that one can make $d_M\left(\pi_M\phi^{k-1}(g'(\omega),\omega),\pi_M\phi^{k-1}(y',\omega)\right)$ and $d_M\left(g'(\omega),y'\right)$ arbitrarily small by taking $k$ large enough. It is worth to point out that the largeness of $k$ is depending on $C(2\alpha_1+4\alpha_2+2\rho)$ only while it is nothing to do with  the choice on specific $\omega$ as long as $\omega\in \Omega\setminus \Omega'$. Now we  choose $k$ large enough so that the following holds
$$\max\left\{d_M\left(\pi_M\phi^{k}(g'(\omega),\omega),\pi_M\phi^{k}(y',\omega)\right),d_M\left(g'(\omega),y'\right)\right\}<C\rho,\ \forall \omega\in\Omega\setminus \Omega'.$$
Thus
\begin{equation}                                              
\max\left\{d_M\left(\pi_M\phi^{k}(g'(\omega),\omega),\tilde \phi^{n+k}(g)(\theta^{k}\omega)\right),d_M\left(g'(\omega),\tilde \phi^{n}(g)(\omega)\right)\right\}<4C\rho,\ \forall \omega\in\Omega\setminus \Omega',
\end{equation}
here we used the fact that $C(2\rho+2\alpha_2)\le 4C\rho$.

Therefore, by using the same argument as in (\ref{E:EstOnOrbit}), we obtain that
\begin{equation}\label{E:EstOnOrbSeg}              
d_M\left(\tilde\phi^i(g')(\theta^i\omega),\tilde \phi^{n+i}(g)(\theta^i\omega)\right)\le 16e^{-\min\{i,k-i\}\lambda}C\rho,\ \forall \ \omega\in \Omega\setminus \Omega', 0\le i\le k.
\end{equation}
Now we are ready to estimate $\left|\hat\Psi'(h_2)-\hat\Psi'(h_1)\right|$:
\begin{align*}
&\left|\hat\Psi(h_2)-\hat\Psi(h_1)\right|\\
\le&\left|\hat\Psi(h_2)-\sum_{i=0}^{n+k}\tilde\Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g))\right|+\left|\hat\Psi(h_1)-\sum_{i=0}^{n}\tilde\Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g))\right|+\left|\sum_{i=n+1}^{n+k}\tilde\Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g))\right|\\
\le &2C'\alpha_2^\alpha+\left|\sum_{i=n+1}^{n+k}\tilde\Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g))\right|\ \left(C'\text{ is the H\"older constant of functional }\hat \Psi'\right)\\
=&2C'\alpha_2^\alpha+\left|\sum_{i=n+1}^{n+k}\tilde\Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g))-\sum_{i=1}^{k}\tilde\Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g'))\right|\ \left(g' \text{ is a periodic point of } \tilde\phi\right)\\
\le& 2C'\alpha_2^\alpha+\sum_{i=1}^k\left|\tilde\Phi(\tilde\phi^{i+n}(g))-\tilde\Phi(\tilde\phi^i(g'))\right|\\
\le&2C'\alpha_2^\alpha+\sum_{i=1}^k\int_{\theta^i(\Omega\setminus \Omega')}\left|\Phi\left(\tilde\phi^{i+n}(g)(\omega),\omega\right)-\Phi\left(\tilde\phi^i(g')(\omega),\omega\right)\right|d\mathbb P\\
&+\sum_{i=1}^{k-N_1}\int_{\theta^i( \Omega')}\left|\Phi\left(\tilde\phi^{i+n}(g)(\omega),\omega\right)-\Phi\left(\tilde\phi^i(g')(\omega),\omega\right)\right|d\mathbb P\\
 &+\sum_{i=k-N_1+1}^{k}\int_{\theta^i( \Omega')}\left|\Phi\left(\tilde\phi^{i+n}(g)(\omega),\omega\right)-\Phi\left(\tilde\phi^i(g')(\omega),\omega\right)\right|d\mathbb P\\
 \le& 2C'\alpha_2^\alpha+\sum_{i=1}^k\int_{\theta^i(\Omega\setminus \Omega')}\|\Phi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}\left(16LC\rho\right)^\alpha e^{-\min\{i,k-i\}\alpha\lambda}d\mathbb P\ \left(\text{by }(\ref{E:EstOnOrbSeg})\right)\\
 &+\sum_{i=1}^{k-N_1}\int_{\theta^i( \Omega')}\|\Phi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}\left(20LC\alpha_1\right)^\alpha e^{-\min\{i,k-N_1-i\}\alpha\lambda}d\mathbb P\ \left(\text{by }(\ref{E:PeriodicShadowg'})\text{ and }(\ref{E:EstOnOrbit})\right)\\
 &+\sum_{i=k-N_1+1}^{k}\int_{\theta^i( \Omega')}2\|\Phi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}d\mathbb P\\
 \le&2C'\alpha_2^\alpha+\frac{2\left(16LC\rho\right)^\alpha}{1-e^{-\alpha\lambda}}\int_{\Omega}\|\Phi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}d\mathbb P+\left(\frac{2\left(20LC\alpha_1\right)^\alpha}{1-e^{-\alpha\lambda}}+2N_1\right)\overline \Phi(\mathbb P(\Omega')),
\end{align*}
where the fact that $0<\alpha_2<\rho<\alpha_1$ is used.

Note that, in the last line of above estimate, $\alpha_1$ and $N_1$ are fixed while $\alpha_2$ can be chosen arbitrarily small which consequentially forces $n$ and $k$ tend to $+\infty$. Thus
\begin{align*}
\left|\hat\Psi(h_2)-\hat\Psi(h_1)\right|\le& L'\overline\Phi(\mathbb P(\Omega'))+L'\rho^\alpha\int_{\Omega}\|\Phi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}d\mathbb P\\
\le& L'\overline\Phi(3\mathbb P(\Omega_1))+L'\rho^\alpha\int_{\Omega}\|\Phi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(M_\omega)}d\mathbb P,
\end{align*}
where $L'=\max\left\{\frac{2\left(16C\right)^\alpha}{1-e^{-\alpha\lambda}},\frac{2\left(20C\alpha_1\right)^\alpha}{1-e^{-\alpha\lambda}}+2N_1\right\}$. The proof is complete.

body_md:
Actually,  this proposition still holds when $\theta$ is assumed to be equicontinuous only. We say $\theta$ is {\bf equicontinuous}  if  there exist $c>1$ and $\delta>0$ such that for any $\omega_1,\omega_2\in \Omega$ with $d_\Omega(\omega_1,\omega_2)<\delta$,
 $$\frac1cd_\Omega(\omega_1,\omega_2)\le d_\Omega(\theta^n\omega_1,\theta^n\omega_2)\le cd_\Omega(\omega_1,\omega_2), \forall n\in \mathbb Z.$$

 When $\theta$ is equicontinuous, if we set
 $$\widetilde{d}_\Omega(\omega_1,\omega_2)=\sup_{n\in \mathbb{Z}}d_{\Omega}(\theta^n \omega_1,\theta^n\omega_2),\, \forall \omega_1,\omega_2\in \Omega,$$
 then $\widetilde{d}_\Omega$ is  a metric on $\Omega$  satisfying that
 \begin{itemize}
 \item $\widetilde{d}_\Omega$ and $d_\Omega$ are equivalent;

 \item $\widetilde{d}_\Omega(\theta^n\omega_1,\theta^n\omega_2)=\widetilde{d}_\Omega(\omega_1,\omega_2)$ for any $\omega_1,\omega_2\in \Omega$
 and $n\in \mathbb{Z}$.
 \end{itemize}
 Therefore, without loss of generality, for an equicontinuous $\theta$, we always assume that
 \begin{equation}\label{E:EquDist}          
 d_\Omega(\theta^n\omega_1,\theta^n\omega_2)=d_\Omega(\omega_1,\omega_2),\ \forall \omega_1,\omega_2\in\Omega\text{ and }n\in \mathbb Z.
 \end{equation}


  For a given $g\in C(\Omega,M)$, we define a neighborhood of its graph as follows.  We consider a finite Borel partition $\xi=\{\xi_i\}_{1\le i\le p}$ of $\Omega$, of which each element contains an nonempty open subset. Such a partition exists because of compactness of $\Omega$. For any $\omega\in\Omega$, we define $\xi(\omega)$ the element in $\xi$ which contains $\omega$, and also denote that
$$B_g(\xi_i,\delta):=\{(x,\omega)|\ \omega\in \xi_i, d_M(x,g(\omega))<\delta\},$$ which induces
a $\delta$-neighborhood of $graph(g)$: $\bigcup_{\xi_i\in\xi} B_g(\xi_i,\delta)$. We denote it by $B_g(\delta)$.

                                                                            

\begin{lem}\label{L:MReturn}          
For any $\delta>0$,                               
there exists $m\in\mathbb N$ such that for any $\xi_i\in\xi$, there exists $(x_i,\omega_i)\in B_g(\xi_i,\delta)$ such that
$$\phi^m(x_i,\omega_i)\in B_g(\xi_i,\delta).$$
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
Since $\phi$ is transitive, there exists $(x_0,\omega_0)$ such that the orbit of $\{\phi^n(x_0,\omega_0)\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ is dense in $M\times \Omega$.
 By the finiteness of the partition, we have that there exist a point $(x,\omega)$ in the interior of $B_g(\xi_1,\delta)$ and  an $m_0\in\mathbb N$ such that
$$\phi^{n_i}(x,\omega)\in \text{interior of }B_g(\xi_i,\delta)\text{ for some }n_i\in[1,m_0],\ \forall i\in[2,p].$$
By the continuity of $\phi$ and the finiteness of the partition, we have that there exists a small open neighbourhood of $(x,\omega)$ in $M\times \Omega$, which is denoted by $U$, such that
$$U\subset B_g(\xi_1,\delta)\text{ and }\phi^{n_i}(U)\subset \text{interior of }B_g(\xi_i,\delta),\ \forall i\in[2,p].$$
 Then, by the transitivity of the system, there exist an $m\in \mathbb N$ and $(x',\omega')\in U$ such that $\phi^m(x',\omega')\in U$. Note that $$\phi^m(\phi^{n_i}(x',\omega'))=\phi^{n_i}(\phi^m(x',\omega'))\in \phi^{n_i}(U) \subset \text{interior of }B_g(\xi_i,\delta),\ \forall i\in[2,p].$$
We complete the proof by letting $(x_1,\omega_1)=(x',\omega')$ and $(x_i,\omega_i)=\phi^{n_i}(x',\omega')$ for $i\in[2,p]$.

\end{proof}

\bigskip

Next, we will construct a $(\upsilon,\delta)$-{\bf pseudo orbit}  for $\upsilon\in \Omega$, $g\in C(\Omega,M)$, and $\delta>0$. Given $\delta>0$, by Lemma \ref{L:MReturn}, there exist $m=m(\delta,g,\phi) >0$ and $(x_i,\omega_i)\in B_g(\xi_i,\delta)$ for $1\le i\le p$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{E:MReturn}          
\phi^m(x_i,  \omega_i)\in  B_g(\xi_i,\delta)\text{ for }1\le i\le p.
\end{equation}
For $l\in\mathbb Z$, suppose that $\theta^{lm}\upsilon\in \xi_{i_l}$, then we define
\begin{equation}\label{E:DefPseOrb}            
(y_j,\upsilon_j)=\begin{cases}
(g(\theta^{lm}\upsilon),\theta^{lm}\upsilon), &\text{ when }j=lm\\
(\pi_M\phi^{j-lm}(x_{i_l},\omega_{i_l}),\theta^j\upsilon),&\text{ when }j\in[lm+1,(l+1)m-1]\\
\end{cases}.
\end{equation}
\begin{lem}\label{L:PseudoOrbit}              
For any $\epsilon'>0$, there exists $\delta'(\phi,g,\epsilon')>0$ such that if $\delta$ and the  diameter of the partition $\xi$  are less than $\delta'$,  the pseudo orbit defined by (\ref{E:DefPseOrb}) starting from $(y,\upsilon)\in graph(g)$  is a $(\upsilon,\epsilon')$-pseudo orbit.
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
Noting that  $g$ is uniformly continuous since $\Omega$ being compact. Therefore, for any $\epsilon_1>0$, there exists $\delta_1>0$ such that for any $\omega_1,\omega_2\in \Omega$ if $d_\Omega(\omega_1,\omega_2)<\delta_1$ then
\begin{equation}\label{E:POEst1}         
  d_M(g(\omega_1),g(\omega_2))<\epsilon_1.
\end{equation}
 Also note that both $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ are uniformly continuous, then for any $\epsilon_2>0$ there exists a $\delta_2>0$ such that for any $(x_1,\omega_1),(x_2,\omega_2)\in M\times \Omega$ once $d((x_1,\omega_1),(x_2,\omega_2))<\delta_2$ the following holds
 \begin{equation}\label{E:POEst2}         
   \max\{d(\phi(x_1,\omega_1),\phi(x_2,\omega_2)),d(\phi^{-1}(x_1,\omega_1),\phi^{-1}(x_2,\omega_2))\}<\epsilon_2.
 \end{equation}
                                                                                                                                                  
                                          
                                                                                                            
               
Note that $d_\Omega(\theta^j\upsilon,\theta^{j-lm}\omega_{i_0})$ is less than the diameter of the partition $\xi$ (which is less than $\delta'(\phi,g,\epsilon')$) for all $j\in[lm,(l+1)m]$ and $l\in \mathbb Z$ by (\ref{E:EquDist}). For  a given $(y,\upsilon)\in graph(g)$ with $\upsilon\in \xi_{i_0}$,  the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item[a)] When $j\in [lm+2,(l+1)m-1]$,  taking $\delta'<\delta_2$,  then (\ref{E:POEst2}) implies that
  \begin{align*}
  d_M(y_j,\pi_M\phi(y_{j-1},\upsilon_{j-1}))
  =&d_M(y_j,\pi_M\phi(y_{j-1},\theta^{j-1}\upsilon))\\
  \le &  d(\phi(y_{j-1},\theta^{j-lm-1}\omega_{i_l}),\phi(y_{j-1},\theta^{j-lm-1}\upsilon_{lm}))\\
  \le& \epsilon_2,
  \end{align*}
  where the fact that $\upsilon_{lm}\in\xi_{i_l}$ is used.
  \item[b)] When $j=lm+1$, taking $\delta'<\frac12 \delta_2$ (thus $\delta<\frac12\delta_2$), then
  $$d\left((x_{i_l},\omega_{i_l}),(g(\theta^{lm}\upsilon),\theta^{lm}\upsilon)\right)<\delta_2.$$ Hence, (\ref{E:POEst2}) implies that
   $$d_M\left(y_j,\pi_M\phi(y_{j-1},\upsilon_{j-1})\right)=d_M\left(\pi_M\phi(x_{i_l},\omega_{i_l}),\pi_M\phi(g(\theta^{lm}\upsilon),\theta^{lm}\upsilon)\right)<\epsilon_2;$$

  \item[c)] For $j=(l+1)m$,  taking $\delta'<\min\{\delta_1,\delta_2\}$, then (\ref{E:POEst1}), (\ref{E:MReturn}), and (\ref{E:POEst2}) implies that
  \begin{align*}
  & d_M(y_j,\pi_M\phi(y_{j-1},\upsilon_{j-1}))\\
  =&d_M\left(g(\theta^j\upsilon),\pi_M\phi(y_{j-1},\upsilon_{j-1})\right)\\
 \le & d_M\left(g(\theta^m\upsilon_{lm}),g(\theta^m\omega_{i_l})\right)+d_M\left(g(\theta^m\omega_{i_l}),\pi_M\phi^m(x_{i_l},\omega_{i_l})\right)\\
    &+d_M(\pi_M\phi^m(x_{i_l},\omega_{i_l}),\pi_M\phi(y_{j-1},\theta^{m-1}\upsilon_{lm}))\\
    \le& \epsilon_1+\delta+d_M(\pi_M\phi(y_{j-1},\theta^{m-1}\omega_{i_l}),\pi_M\phi(y_{j-1},\theta^{m-1}\upsilon_{lm}))\\
    \le&\epsilon_1+\delta+\epsilon_2.
  \end{align*}
\end{enumerate}
Therefore, the required estimate can be achieved  if we choose $,\epsilon_1+\delta +\epsilon_2<\epsilon'$ and take a $\delta'>0$  which satisfies all the proposed conditions  in a), b), and c) above. So for such $\delta'>0$ if $\delta$ and $diam(\xi)$ are less than $\delta'$, the  pseudo-orbit defined by (\ref{E:DefPseOrb}) is a $(\upsilon,\epsilon')$-pseudo orbit.

\end{proof}

\begin{lem}\label{L:LipG}       
For any $\epsilon'>0$ and $L>0$, there exists $\delta'(\phi,L,\epsilon')>0$ such that for any $g\in C(\Omega,M)$ with $Lip\ g\le L$ if $\delta$ and the  diameter of the partition $\xi$  are less than $\delta'$,  then the pseudo orbit defined by (\ref{E:DefPseOrb}) starting from $(y,\upsilon)\in graph(g)$  is a $(\upsilon,\epsilon')$-pseudo orbit.
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
In the proof of Lemma \ref{L:PseudoOrbit} above, the dependence of $\delta'$ on $g$ is given by  (\ref{E:POEst1}) which appears in part c). So the exact property of ``$g$'' being involved in this lemma is how uniformly continuous it is. Therefore, under the setting of the current lemma, the exactly same argument can be applied here, in which ``$\delta'$'' depends on the Lipchitz constant ``$L$'' rather than the choice of particular map ``$g$''. The detailed proof is omitted.
\end{proof}
Now we are ready to prove Proposition \ref{P:DensePeriodicOrb1}. For a given small $\epsilon>0$ and $g\in C(\Omega,M)$, choose $0<\beta<\min\{\frac12\epsilon,\beta_0\}$. By Lemma \ref{L:LShad}, there exists a corresponding $\alpha>0$ for $\beta$. Then, by applying Lemma \ref{L:MReturn} and \ref{L:PseudoOrbit}, for $\epsilon'=\alpha$ there exists a $\delta'>0$ such that for any $\upsilon\in\Omega$ and $\delta\in(0,\delta')$, there exists $m\in \mathbb N$ which is depending on $\delta,g,\phi$ only and a $(\upsilon,\alpha)$-pseudo orbit defined by (\ref{E:DefPseOrb}), which is denoted by $\{(y_i,\theta^n\upsilon)\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}$, such that
$$(y_{km},\theta^{km}\upsilon)\in graph(g),\ \forall k\in\mathbb Z.$$
Define  $g_i:\Omega\to M$ for $i\in \mathbb Z$ as follows
$$g_j(\upsilon)=\begin{cases}
g(\upsilon), &\text{ when }j=lm\\
\pi_M\phi^{j-lm}(x_{i_l},\omega_{i_l}),&\text{ when }j\in[lm+1,(l+1)m-1]\text{ and }\theta^{-(j-lm)}\upsilon\in \xi_{i_l}\\
\end{cases}.$$
It is clear that each $g_i$ is measurable since $g_i$ is either a continuous function or a pre-image of a simple function under continuous iterations. Also note that
$$(y_i,\theta^n\upsilon)\in graph(g_i),\ \forall\upsilon\in\Omega\text{ and }i\in \mathbb Z.$$
Thus $\{g_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ is an $\alpha$-pseudo orbit of $\tilde\phi$. By applying Lemma \ref{L:LShad}, there is a true orbit $\{\tilde\phi(\tilde g)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ which is $\beta$-shadowing $\{g_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$. The uniqueness of such a $\tilde g$ and the periodicity of $\{g_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ imply that $\tilde g$ is a periodic point of $\tilde \phi$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Actually, what was required for the driven system is the following: $\Omega$ is connected, and for any $n\in\mathbb N$, $\theta^n$ is uniquely ergodic and $\mathbb P$ is the ergodic probability measure.

By Proposition \ref{P:DensePeriodicOrb1}, we have that for any  $g\in C(\Omega,M)$ and $\epsilon>0$, there exists a  random periodic point $\tilde g\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ satisfying (\ref{E:LInfiClose}). For this $\tilde g$,  let
\begin{equation}\label{E:XTg}       
X_{\tilde g}= \bigcup_{\omega\in\Omega}\{(x,\omega)| x\in \overline{W^u(\tilde g(\omega),\omega)}\},
\end{equation}
where $\overline{W^u(\tilde g(\omega),\omega)}$ is the closure of the global unstable manifold of $(\tilde g(\omega),\omega)$ in $(M,\omega)$.   We first require the following condition on the parameters:

{\bf C1:} By taking $\epsilon$ small enough, we require that $\epsilon<\frac12 \delta$ where $\delta$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:LocCoor} corresponding to $\frac12\epsilon_0$ with $\epsilon_0$ being a prefixed small number.

                                               
                                                    
            
              
 
            

First, we show that
\begin{equation}\label{E:OpenClose}            
X_{\tilde g}=M\times \Omega.
\end{equation}
                                             
                                                         
                                                                                                                         
            

The next lemma is the key result needed in the proof:
 \begin{lem}\label{L:ContiG}         
  For any $(x,\omega)\in M\times\Omega$, $g\in C(\Omega,M)$, and an open neighborhood $V\subset \Omega$ of $\omega$,  there exist an nonempty open set $A\subset\Omega\setminus\{\omega\}$ with $\Omega\setminus A\subset V$ and a function $g'\in C(\Omega,M)$ such that
 \begin{equation}\label{E:g'}     
 g'(\omega)=x\text{ and }g'|_A=g|_A.
 \end{equation}
 \end{lem}
 The proof of this lemma may be standard, however we give it here for the sake of completeness.
 \begin{proof}
 First, there exists a path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$ such that $\gamma(0)=g(\omega)$ and $\gamma(1)=x$. Note that there exist finitely many numbers $0=s_0<s_1<s_2<\cdots<s_n=1$ such that $\gamma(s_i)$ and $\gamma(s_{i+1})$ are in a same chart  of the atlas of $M$, say $(U_i,\psi_i)$, for all $i=0,\cdots, n-1$.
 Consider an open ball $B(\omega,R_1)$ centered at $\omega$ in $\Omega$,  with $R_1$ small enough so that $B(\omega,R_1)\subset V$,  $\mathbb P(\overline{B(\omega,R_1)})<1$ and $g(B(\omega,R_1))\subset U_1$. Note that  $\{\omega\}$ and $\Omega\setminus B(\omega,\frac12 R_1)$ are disjoint closed sets. By Urysohn's lemma, there exists a continuous function $f_1:\Omega\to[0,1]$ such that
 $$f_1|_{\Omega\setminus B(\omega,\frac12R_1)}=0\text{ and }f_1(\omega)=1.$$
 Then, the following is well defined
 $$g_1(\upsilon)=\begin{cases}g_0(\upsilon),&\text{ if }\upsilon\notin B(\omega,\frac12R_1)\\
\psi_1^{-1}\left[ f_1(\upsilon)\psi_1(\gamma(s_1))+(1-f_1(\upsilon))\psi_1(g_0(\upsilon))\right],&\text{ if }\upsilon\in B(\omega,\frac 12R_1)\end{cases},$$
where we set $g_0=g$ for the sake of convenience.

 It is obvious that $g_1$ is continuous and satisfies that
 $$g_1(\omega)=\gamma(s_1)\text{ and }A_1:=\{\omega|g_1(\omega)=g(\omega)\}\text{ contains an open set}.$$
 Inductively, we can construct $g_{i+1}$ based on $g_i$ by using   exactly the same argument above to ensure the following:
 $$g_{i+1}(\omega)=\gamma(s_{i+1})\text{ and }A_{i+1}:=\{\omega|g_1(\omega)=g(\omega)\}\text{ contains an open set}.$$
 To guarantee the existence of  $A$, it is sufficient to take $R_{i+1}<R_i$. In this case, we can take $A=\Omega\setminus \overline{B(\omega,\frac12R_1)}$.

 \end{proof}

 \begin{rem}
 Actually, it is not hard to see that $\mathbb P(A)$ can be taken arbitrarily close to $1$ since $\mathbb P$ is not  atomic.
 \end{rem}

Now, we are ready to prove Theorem \ref{T:Spectrum11}.
For an arbitrary $(x,\omega)\in  M\times\Omega$, and $g$ chosen at the beginning of the proof, by Lemma \ref{L:ContiG}, there exists $g'\in C(\Omega,M)$ satisfying (\ref{E:g'}).  For a small $\epsilon'\in (0,\frac12\delta)$, where $\delta$ is as in C1). We apply Proposition \ref{P:DensePeriodicOrb1} to $g'$, and then derive that there exists a random periodic point $\tilde g'\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{E:ClosePerOrb}              
\sup_{\upsilon\in A}\{d_M(\tilde g'(\upsilon),\tilde g(\upsilon))\}\le 2\epsilon',
\end{equation}
where $\tilde g$ is the periodic point in (\ref{E:XTg}).
Let $m$ and $m'$ be the periods of $\{graph(\tilde g)\}$ and $\{graph(\tilde g')\}$ respectively. Note that $\theta^{-mm'}$   is $\mathbb P$-ergodic since $\theta$ is invertible and $\theta^{mm'}$ is $\mathbb P$-ergodic, and each $\omega'\in\Omega$ is a $\theta^{mm'}$-minimal point. That means that there is an infinite increasing sequence of positive integers, $0<n_1<n_2<n_3<\cdots$, such that $\theta^{-n_imm'}\omega\in A$ for $i\ge 1$ as long as $A$ has nonempty interior.

For $i\ge 1$, let
\begin{align*}
x'_i&=[\pi_M\phi^{-n_imm'}(\tilde g'(\omega),\omega),\tilde g(\theta^{-n_imm'}\omega)]_{\theta^{-n_imm'}\omega}\\
&=W^s_{\frac{\epsilon_0}2}(\phi^{-n_imm'}(\tilde g'(\omega),\omega))\bigcap W^u_{\frac{\epsilon_0}2}(\tilde g(\theta^{-n_imm'}\omega),\theta^{-n_imm'}\omega),
\end{align*}
which is well defined by the choice of $\epsilon_0,\epsilon'$ and (\ref{E:ClosePerOrb}).



Note that, by Lemma \ref{L:InvMani}, we have that
$$\lim_{i\to\infty}\phi^{n_imm'}(x'_i,\theta^{-n_imm'}\omega)\to (\tilde g'(\omega),\omega)\text{ and }\phi^{n_imm'}(x'_i,\theta^{-n_imm'}\omega)\in W^u(\tilde g(\omega),\omega),$$
which implies that
$$(\tilde g'(\omega),\omega)\in \overline{W^u(\tilde g(\omega),\omega)}\subset X_{\tilde g}.$$
Since $d_M(g'(\omega),x)<\epsilon'$ and $\epsilon'$ can be taken arbitrarily small, we have that $(x,\omega)\in X_{\tilde g}$. Thus (\ref{E:OpenClose}) holds by the arbitrariness of $(x,\omega)$. \\

                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                    
                                                                                          
             


Finally, we show that $\phi$ is {\bf topological mixing on fibers}.
Roughly speaking, the proof is based on the fact that the global stable manifold of a  random periodic point is dense in $M\times\Omega$.
The following lemma is the key  to derive the mixing property.
\begin{lem}\label{L:Converging}             
For any $\epsilon_1>0$ and $g\in C(\Omega,M)$, there exists $\delta_1>0$ such that the following holds:\\
For any  random periodic point $graph(\tilde g)\in B_g(\delta_1)$ (with period $l$), $\epsilon'_1>0$ and $h\in C(\Omega,M)$,
 there exist $N\in\mathbb N$, and a measurable function $h_1:\Omega\to M$ satisfying that
$$graph(h_1)\subset B_{h}(\epsilon'_1)\text{ and }\phi^{nl}(graph(h_1))\subset B_g(\epsilon_1),\forall n>N.$$
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
Here we only need to take $\delta_1\in(0,\frac16\epsilon_1)$ small enough such that any $2\delta_1$-pseudo orbit of $\tilde\phi$ can be $\frac13\epsilon_1$-shadowed by a unique true orbit. This can be done by Lemma \ref{L:LShad}. For the rest of the proof of this lemma, such a $\delta_1$ is fixed.

 It is not hard to see that the existence of $\tilde g$ follows from Proposition \ref{P:DensePeriodicOrb1} directly. For an arbitrarily fixed $\omega\in\Omega$, by Lemma \ref{L:ContiG}, there exist an nonempty  open set $A_\omega\subset \Omega$ and $g'_\omega\in C(\Omega,M)$  such that
 \begin{equation}\label{E:g'gAomega}            
 g'_\omega(\omega)=h(\omega)\text{ and }g'_\omega|_{A_\omega}=g|_{A_\omega}.
 \end{equation}
  By applying Proposition \ref{P:DensePeriodicOrb1}, we have that there is a random periodic point $\tilde g'_\omega\in L^\infty(\Omega, M)$ with period $l_\omega$ such that
  \begin{equation}\label{E:TilG'omega}             
  graph(\tilde g'_\omega)\in B_{g'_\omega}\left(\frac13\epsilon'_1\right),
  \end{equation}
  where, without loss of generality, we assume that $\epsilon'_1\in(0,\delta_1)$.


  Let $B_\omega\subset A_\omega$ be an open ball  in $\Omega$ with radius $r_\omega>0$, and $C_\omega$ be an open neighborhood of $\omega$  with radius $\frac12r_\omega$. This $r_\omega$ is taken additionally small to ensure the following inequality
  \begin{equation}\label{E:GomegaHmu}            
  |g'_\omega(\upsilon)-h(\upsilon)|<\frac13\epsilon'_1,\ \forall \upsilon\in C_\omega.
  \end{equation}
  Since $\theta^{l_\omega l}$ is an isometric map on $\Omega$ and any nonempty open subset of $\Omega$ is not $\mathbb P$-null set, there is an infinite set $I_\omega\subset\mathbb N$ such that the following holds
  $$\theta^{nl_\omega l}(C_\omega)\subset B_\omega,\ \forall n\in I_\omega.$$
  For  $\upsilon\in C_\omega$ and $n\in I_\omega$, define that
                                                               
                              
                                                      
                                                           
                 
  $$(y_i,\upsilon_i)_{n}=\begin{cases}
  \phi^i(\tilde g'_\omega(\upsilon),\upsilon)&\text{ when }i< nl_\omega l\\
  \phi^{i-nl_\omega l}(\tilde g(\theta^{nl_\omega l}\upsilon),\theta^{nl_\omega l}\upsilon)&\text{ when }i\ge nl_\omega l
  \end{cases}.$$
  It is clearly $\{(y_i,\upsilon_i)_{n}\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ is an $(\upsilon,\frac32\delta_1)$-pseudo orbit because of (\ref{E:TilG'omega}) and (\ref{E:g'gAomega}). By the choice of $\epsilon_1$ and $\delta_1$ at the beginning of the proof, we have that there exists a unique true orbit $\{\phi^i(z_{\omega,n}(\upsilon),\upsilon)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ which is $(\upsilon,\frac13\epsilon_1)$-shadowing $\{(y_i,\upsilon_i)_n\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$. Note that $\delta_1+\frac32\delta_1+\frac13\epsilon_1<\frac34\epsilon_1$, then we have that
  \begin{equation}\label{E:1}    
  \phi^{ml}(z_{\omega,n}(\upsilon),\upsilon)\in B_g\left(\frac34\epsilon_1\right),\ \forall m\ge nl_\omega.
  \end{equation}
  By Lemma \ref{L:ContinousShadowing}, there exists $N_\omega\in \mathbb N$ such that if we choose $nl_\omega> N_\omega$, then
  $$d_M\left(z_{\omega,n}(\upsilon),\tilde g'_\omega(\upsilon)\right)<\frac13\epsilon'_1,$$
  which together with (\ref{E:TilG'omega}) and (\ref{E:GomegaHmu}) implies that
    \begin{equation}\label{E:2}    
  d_M(z_{\omega,n}(\upsilon),h(\upsilon))<\epsilon'_1.
  \end{equation}
                                    
                                                                                            
                     
                                  
                             
                 
  So far, we have defined a measurable function $z_{\omega,n}:C_\omega\to M$ with an integer $N_\omega\in \mathbb N$ ($n$ is required to be larger than $N_\omega$)  satisfying (\ref{E:1}) and (\ref{E:2}) for all $\upsilon\in C_\omega$. We remark here that the measurability of $z_\omega$ can be proved exactly in the  same way as the argument in the proof of Proposition \ref{P:DensePeriodicOrb1}, thus is omitted here.

  Note that $\{C_\omega\}_{\omega\in\Omega}$ forms an open cover of the compact set $\Omega$. Thus there is an finite open sub-cover which is denoted by $\{C_{\omega_1},\cdots C_{\omega_s}\}$. The proof is completed if we take $N=\max\{N_{\omega_1},\cdots, N_{\omega_s}\}$ and define
  $$h_1(\omega)=\begin{cases}
  z_{\omega_1}(\omega)&\text{ when }\omega\in C_{\omega_1}\\
  z_{\omega_i}(\omega)&\text{ when }\omega\in  C_{\omega_i}\setminus \bigcup_{1\le j\le i-1}C_{\omega_j},\ \forall 2\le i\le s
  \end{cases}.
  $$
\end{proof}




Let $U$ and $V$ be nonempty open sets in $M$ with an $x\in U$ and a $y\in V$ fixed. Then there exists $\epsilon_2>0$ such that
$$B_M(x,\epsilon_2)\subset U\text{ and }B_M(y,\epsilon_2)\subset V.$$
Applying  Lemma \ref{L:Converging} by taking $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2$ and $g=h_y$ where $h_y(\omega)=y$ for all $\omega\in\Omega$, we can derive a $\delta_2>0$ correspondingly. By Proposition \ref{P:DensePeriodicOrb1}, there exists a  random periodic point $graph(\tilde h_y)\in B_{h_y}(\delta_2)$ with period $p$.
Since $\phi$ is homeomorphism, for any $i\in\mathbb N$, $\phi^{i}(U\times \Omega)$ is open in $M\times\Omega$ while $\phi^{i}(graph(h_x))\subset \phi^{i}(U\times\Omega)$ is compact.
Therefore, there exists $\epsilon_3\in(0,\epsilon_2)$ such that
$$B_{g_i}(\epsilon_3)\subset \phi^{i}(U\times \Omega), \ \forall 0\le i \le p-1,$$
where $g_i(:=\tilde\phi(h_x))\in C(\Omega, M)$. Applying Lemma \ref{L:Converging} $p$ times, we have that there exist $\{N_0,\cdots, N_{p-1}\} \subset \mathbb N$ and measurable functions $\{g'_i:\Omega\to M\}_{0\le i\le p-1}$ such that for all $0\le i\le p-1$ the following hold
\begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:3}    
&graph(g'_i)\subset B_{g_i}(\epsilon_3)\subset \phi^{i}(U\times\Omega)\\
&\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\text{and}\\
&\phi^{np}(graph(g'_i))\subset B_{h_y}(\epsilon_2)\subset V\times \Omega,\forall n>N_i.
\end{split}
\end{align}
Obviously, (\ref{E:3}) holds if we replace $N_i$ by $N:=\max\{N_0,\cdots, N_{p-1}\}$. Therefore, for any $m\in\mathbb N$, if $m=np+j$ where $n>N$ and $j\in[0,p)$, then
$$\phi^{np}(graph(g'_i))\subset B_g(\epsilon_2)\bigcap \phi^{m-j}(\phi^{j}(U\times \Omega))\subset V\times \Omega \bigcap \phi^{m}(U\times \Omega),$$
which implies that for any $\omega\in\Omega$,
$$\phi^{m}(U\times \{\omega\})\cap V\times \{\theta^{m}\omega\}\neq \emptyset.$$
  This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{T:Spectrum11}.

  \qed

title: Lemma
body_md: $\phi$ is Anosov on fibers and transitive.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f_\omega \binom{x}{y}= A\binom{x}{y}+h(\omega)$ for $\omega\in \mathbb{T}$. Then $\phi\left(\binom{x}{y},\omega\right)=\left(f_\omega \binom{x}{y},\omega+\alpha\right)$.
Note that $Df_\omega \binom{x}{y}=A$ for any $(\binom{x}{y},\omega)\in \mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T}$ and $A$ is a hyperbolic matrix. Hence $(\mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T},\phi)$ is Anosov on fibers.

Let $\mu$ be the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T}$. To show that $T$ is transitive, it is sufficient to show that $(\mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T}}, \phi,\mu)$ is an ergodic measure-preserving system. First, it is clear that $(\mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T}}, \phi,\mu)$ is a measure-preserving system. In the following we show that $(\mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T}}, \phi,\mu)$ is ergodic.

Let $f\in L^2(\mu)$ with $f\circ \phi=f$ $\mu$-a.e.. Let
$$f\left(\binom{x}{y},\omega\right)=\sum_{(k,l,n)\in \mathbb{Z}^3} c_{k,l,n} e^{2\pi i \left(k\omega+(l,n)\binom{x}{y}\right)}$$
be the Fourier series of $f$ on $\mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T}$. Then
$$\sum_{(k,l,n)\in \mathbb{Z}^3} |c_{k,l,n}|^2=\|f\|_{L^2(\mu)}<+\infty.$$
Fix $(n',l')\in \mathbb{Z}^2$. For any $g\in L^2(m_{\mathbb{T}})$, where $m_{\mathbb{T}}$ is the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{T}$,
we have
\begin{align*}
&\hskip0.5cm \int \left( \sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} c_{k,l',n'} e^{2\pi i k \omega}\right) g(\omega) d m_{\mathbb{T}}(\omega)\\
&=\int \left(\sum_{(k,l,n)\in \mathbb{Z}^3} c_{k,l,n} e^{2\pi i \left(k\omega+(l,n)\binom{x}{y}\right)}\right) g(\omega)e^{-2\pi i(l',n')\binom{x}{y}} d \mu\left(\binom{x}{y},\omega\right) \\
&=\int f\left(\binom{x}{y},\omega\right) g(\omega)e^{-2\pi i(l',n')\binom{x}{y}} d \mu\left(\binom{x}{y},\omega\right)\\
&=\int f\left(\phi^{-1}\left(\binom{x}{y},\omega\right)\right)  g(\omega)e^{-2\pi i(l',n')\binom{x}{y}} d \mu\left(\binom{x}{y},\omega\right)  \\
&=\int f\left(\binom{x}{y},\omega\right) g(\omega+\alpha)e^{-2\pi i(l',n')\left(A\binom{x}{y}+h(\omega)\right)} d \mu\left(\binom{x}{y},\omega\right)\\
&= \int \left(\sum_{(k,l,n)\in \mathbb{Z}^3} c_{k,l,n} e^{2\pi i \left(k\omega+(l,n)\binom{x}{y}\right)}\right) g(\omega+\alpha)e^{-2\pi i(l',n')\left(A\binom{x}{y}+h(\omega)\right)} d \mu\left(\binom{x}{y},\omega\right)\\
&=\int\left( \sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} c_{k,(l',n')A} e^{2\pi i k \omega}\right)e^{-2\pi i (l',n')h(\omega)} g(\omega+\alpha) d m_{\mathbb{T}}(\omega)\\
&=\int \left( \sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} c_{k,(l',n')A} e^{2\pi i k (\omega-\alpha)}\right)e^{-2\pi i (l',n')h(\omega-\alpha)} g(\omega) d m_{\mathbb{T}}(\omega).
\end{align*}
Since the above equality holds for any $g\in L^2(m_{\mathbb{T}})$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq-11}
 \sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} c_{k,l',n'} e^{2\pi i k \omega}= \left( \sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} c_{k,(l',n')A} e^{2\pi i k (\omega-\alpha)}\right)e^{-2\pi i (l',n')h(\omega-\alpha)}
\end{equation}
in $L^2(m_{\mathbb{T}})$.
Thus
$$\int \left| \sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} c_{k,l',n'} e^{2\pi i k \omega}\right|^2 d m_{\mathbb{T}}(\omega)=
\int \left|\left( \sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} c_{k,(l',n')A} e^{2\pi i k (\omega-\alpha)}\right)e^{-2\pi i (l',n')h(\omega-\alpha)}\right|^2 d m_{\mathbb{T}}(\omega).
$$
Hence
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} |c_{k,l',n'}|^2=\sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} |c_{k,(l',n')A}|^2.
\end{equation*}
When $(l',n')\neq (0,0)$, $(l',n')A^m\neq (l',n')A^k$ for $m,k\in \mathbb{N}$ with $m\neq k$.
Hence if $(l',n')\neq (0,0)$ then for any $N\in \mathbb{N}$,
\begin{align*}
\sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} |c_{k,l',n'}|^2=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} |c_{k,(l',n')A^i}|^2 \le \frac{1}{N} \sum_{(k,l,n)\in \mathbb{Z}^3} |c_{k,l,n}|^2\le \frac{1}{N} \|f\|_{L^2(\mu)}.
\end{align*}
Let $N\nearrow +\infty$, we get $\sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} |c_{k,l',n'}|^2=0$ for $(l',n')\neq (0,0)$.
When $(l',n')= (0,0)$, by \eqref{eq-11} we have
$$\sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} c_{k,0,0} e^{2\pi i k \omega}=\sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} c_{k,0,0}e^{-2\pi i k\alpha} e^{2\pi i k \omega}$$
in $L^2(m_{\mathbb{T}})$.
Thus
$c_{k,0,0}=c_{k,0,0}e^{-2\pi i k\alpha}$ for $k\in \mathbb{Z}$. When $k\neq 0$, we have $c_{k,0,0}=0$ as $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\setminus \mathbb{Q}$.
Summing over we get $f=c_{0,0,0}$. This shows that $(\mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{T}^2\times \mathbb{T}}, \phi,\mu)$ is ergodic. The proof of this lemma is complete.

body_md:
\label{ex-lem-2} Let $deg(h_i)=n_i$ for $i=1,2$. If $n_2$ is odd number, then there are no $g\in C(\mathbb{T},\mathbb{T}^2)$  and positive integer $n$ such that

title: Proof
body_md:
If this is not true, then there are  $g(\omega)=\binom{g_1(\omega)}{g_2(\omega)}\in C(\mathbb{T},\mathbb{T}^2)$  and positive integer $n$ such that
$\phi^n (graph(g))=graph(g)$, i.e.
$$ \phi^n(g(\omega),\omega)=(g(\omega+n\alpha),\omega+n\alpha)$$
for $\omega\in \mathbb{T}$.
Let $deg(g_i)=k_i$ for $i=1,2$. Note that
$$\phi^n(g(\omega),\omega)=\left(A^n\binom{g_1(\omega)}{g_2(\omega)}+A^{n-1}\binom{h_1(\omega)}{h_2(\omega)}+\cdots+\binom{h_1(\omega+(n-1)\alpha)}{h_2(\omega+(n-1)\alpha)},\omega+n\alpha\right)$$
Hence
\begin{align*}
&\binom{g_1(\omega+n\alpha)}{g_2(\omega+n\alpha)}\\=&A^n\binom{g_1(\omega)}{g_2(\omega)}
+A^{n-1}\binom{h_1(\omega)}{h_2(\omega)}+A^{n-2}\binom{h_1(\omega+\alpha)}{h_2(\omega+\alpha)}+\cdots+\binom{h_1(\omega+(n-1)\alpha)}{h_2(\omega+(n-1)\alpha)}.
\end{align*}
Compare the degree of continuous functions from $\mathbb{T}$ to $\mathbb{T}$ appearing in the above equation,  we have
$$\binom{k_1}{k_2}=A^n\binom{k_1}{k_2}
+A^{n-1}\binom{n_1}{n_2}+A^{n-2}\binom{n_1}{n_2}+\cdots+\binom{n_1}{n_2}.$$
That is
$$(I-A^n)\binom{k_1}{k_2}=(I+A+\cdots+A^{n-1})\binom{n_1}{n_2}.$$
Since $\det(I-A^n)\neq 0$ and $(I-A)(I+A+\cdots+A^{n-1})=I-A^n$,  we have
$$(I-A)\binom{k_1}{k_2}=\binom{n_1}{n_2}.$$
This implies $k_1=-\frac{n_2}{2}\not \in \mathbb{Z}$, a contradiction. The proof is complete.

body_md:
Unlike the case of S1) systems, the proof for S2) is based on the measure preserving property of $f_\omega$, which leads to a much more direct approach.

 For a given $\omega\in \Omega$, an open subset $V\subset M$, and a  real number $r>0$, we inductively define a sequence of subsets $V^r_n(\omega)\subset M$, $n=0,1,2,\cdots$ as follows:
 \begin{equation}\label{E:V_n}      
 V^r_n(\omega)=\begin{cases}
 V,&n=0\\
 \cup_{x\in f_{\theta^{n-1}\omega}(V^r_{n-1}(\omega))}B_M(x,r),&n>1
 \end{cases},
 \end{equation}
 where $B_M(x,r)$ is the ball in $M$ with radius $r$ centered at $x$. It is not hard to see that each $V^r_n(\omega)$ is open and $\{\nu(V^r_n(\omega))\}_{n=0,1,\cdots}$ is non-decreasing  on both $n$ and $r$ since $\nu$ is $f$-invariant and $f$ is invertible.  Thus $\lim_{n\to\infty}\nu(V^r_n(\omega))$ exists.

 Next, we show that
 \begin{equation}\label{E:LimVn}        
  \forall\ r>0, \exists\ N(\omega)>0 \text{ such that }\forall\ n\ge N(\omega), V^r_n(\omega)=M.
 \end{equation}
 Since $supp\ \nu=M$, we know that any open subset of $M$ is not a $\nu$-null set. Additionally, because $M$ is compact, for any $R>0$, $M$ can be  covered by finitely many balls with radius $\frac13R$, each of which has a positive $\nu$-measure. Thus, \begin{equation}\label{E:NuInf}                
 \forall\ R>0, \exists\ \epsilon>0, \text{ such that }\forall\ x\in M,\ \nu(B_M(x,R))>\epsilon.
 \end{equation}
 For a given $n\ge 1$, let $t^r_n(\omega)=\min\{\sup\{d_H(x,f_{\theta^{n-1}\omega}(V^r_{n-1}(\omega))|\ x\in M\},r\}$, where for $x\in M$ and $A\subset M$  $$d_H(x,A):=\inf\{d_M(x,y)|\ y\in A\}$$ is the Hausdoff distance. Since $d_H(x,V^r_n(\omega))$ is continuous on $x$ and $M$ is connected, we have that there exists $x'\in M$ such that $$\frac12t^r_n(\omega)< d_H(x',f_{\theta^{n-1}\omega}(V^r_{n-1}(\omega)))<r.$$
 Therefore, $B\left(x',\frac12t^r_n(\omega)\right)\subset V^r_n(\omega)\setminus f_{\theta^{n-1}\omega}(V^r_{n-1}(\omega))$ which implies that
 $$\nu \left(B_M\left(x',\frac12t^r_n(\omega)\right)\right)\le \nu(V^r_n(\omega))-\nu(f_{\theta^{n-1}\omega}(V^r_{n-1}(\omega)))=\nu(V^r_n(\omega))-\nu(V^r_{n-1}(\omega)(\omega)).$$
 Because of the existence of  $\lim_{n\to\infty} \nu (V^r_n(\omega))$ and (\ref{E:NuInf}), we have that
 $$\lim_{n\to\infty} t_n^r=0.$$
 By the definition of $V_n^r(\omega)$ as in (\ref{E:V_n}), once $t_n^r<r$, $V_n^r(\omega)=M$, thus (\ref{E:LimVn}) holds. \\

 Now, we are ready to show that S2)-type systems are topological mixing on fibers.

 Let $U_1, U_2\subset M$ be two nonempty open sets. Choose two open balls $B_M(x_i,3R)\subset U_i$, $i=1,2$, with $R>0$. Applying Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing} by setting $\beta=R$, we have an $\alpha>0$, such that any $(\omega,\alpha)$-pseudo orbit can be $(\omega,\beta)$-shadowed by a true orbit.

  For a given $\omega\in\Omega$, take $V=B_M(x_1,R)$ and $r=\alpha$, and define $V^r_n(\omega)$ as in (\ref{E:V_n}). By (\ref{E:LimVn}), there exists an $N_1(\omega)$ such that for any $n\ge N_1(\omega)$, $V_n^r(\omega)=M$. By continuity of $\phi$, we have that for any $\omega\in\Omega$, there exists $\delta(\omega)>0$ such that the following holds:
 $$\forall\ \omega'\in B_\Omega(\omega,\delta(\omega))\text{ and }n\ge N_1(\omega)+1, \ V^r_n(\omega') =M,$$
 where $B_\Omega(\omega,\delta(\omega))$ is the ball in $\Omega$ with radius $\delta(\omega)$ centered at $\omega$.

 Since $\Omega$ is compact, and $\{B_\Omega(\omega,\delta(\omega))\}_{\omega\in\Omega}$ forms an open cover on $M$, there exists a finite sub-cover, $\{B_\Omega(\omega_j,\delta(\omega_j)\}_{1\le j\le q},\ q\in\mathbb N$. Take $N=\max\{N_1(\omega_1),\cdots, N_1(\omega_q)\}+1$, then the following holds
 \begin{equation}\label{E:UniformN}           
  \forall\ \omega\in\Omega, \text{ if } n\ge N, \text{ then } V^r_n(\omega)=M.
  \end{equation}
 Next, we show that
 \begin{equation}\label{E:TMix}       
\forall\ \omega\in\Omega\text{ and }n\ge N,\  \phi(n,U_1\times\{\omega\})\cap U_2\times\{\theta^n\omega\}\neq \emptyset.
 \end{equation}
 This can be done by constructing an $(\omega,r)$-pseudo orbit, $\{(y'_{n,i},\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$, connecting two balls $B_M(x_1,R)\times \{\omega\}$ and $B_M(x_2,R)\times \{\theta^n\omega\}$, which is $(\omega,R)$-shadowed by a true orbit \[\{(y_{n,i},\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}.\] Thus this true orbit,  $\{(y_{n,i},\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$, will hit both $B_M(x_1,3R)\times \{\omega\}$ and $B_M(x_2,3R)\times \{\theta^n\omega\}$. Hence (\ref{E:TMix}) holds. Actually, the existence of such an $(\omega,r)$-pseudo orbits ($\forall\ \omega\in \Omega$), $\{(y'_{n,i},\theta^i\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$, follows from (\ref{E:UniformN}), which can be constructed in the following:

 For any $n\ge N$ and $\omega\in\Omega$, since $V_N^r(\omega)=M$, we have that there exists $z_{N-1}(\omega)\in V_{N-1}^r(\omega)$ such that
 $$\pi_M\phi^{-(n-N)}(x_2,\theta^n\omega)\in B_M(f_{\theta^{N-1}\omega}z_{N-1}(\omega),r).$$
 Inductively, we have that for any $i\in\{0,\cdots, N-2\}$, there exists $z_i(\omega)\in V_i^r(\omega)$ such that
 $$z_{i+1}(\omega)\in B_M(f_{\theta^i\omega}z_i(\omega),r).$$
 Also note that $V_0^r(\omega)=B_M(x_1,R)$, then we have that $\{z_i(\omega)\}_{1 \le i\le N-1}$ satisfies the following properties:
 \begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:ConnectX1X2}              
  &d_M(z_0(\omega),x_1)<r;\\
  &d_M(z_{i+1}(\omega), f_{\theta^i\omega}z_i(\omega))<r,\ 0\le i\le N-2;\\
  &d_M\left(\pi_M\phi^{-(n-N)}(x_2,\theta^n\omega),f_{\theta^{N-1}\omega}z_{N-1}(\omega)\right)<r.
  \end{split}
   \end{align}
We define
$$
y'_{n,i}=\begin{cases}
\pi_M\phi^i(x_1,\omega),&i\le -1\\
z_i(\omega),&0\le i\le N-1\\
\pi_M\phi^{i-n}(x_2,\theta^n\omega), &i\ge N
\end{cases}.
$$
By (\ref{E:ConnectX1X2}), it is not hard to see that the above $y'_{n,i}$'s  fit all the requirements. The proof is  complete.

title: Proof
body_md:
Denote $\mathbb R^{2+}:=\left\{(x,y)\in \mathbb R^2\setminus \{(0,0)\}\Big|\ x\ge 0, y\ge 0\right\}$. For any $v_i=\left(\begin{matrix}x_i\\y_i\end{matrix}\right)\in \mathbb R^{2+}$, $i=1,2$, by a straightforward computation, we have that
 $$\sin\angle(v_1,v_2)=\left| \frac{y_2x_1-y_1x_2}{\sqrt{x_1^2+y_1^2}\sqrt{x_2^2+y_2^2}}\right|,$$
 where $ \angle(v_1,v_2)$ is the angle between $v_1$ and $v_2$. \\
                                                                                                                                    

 By a straightforward computation, we have that, for any $j\in\{1,\cdots,p\}$, $i=1,2$,
 \begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:Expan&Contrac}                
& |A_jv_i|=\sqrt{(a_j^2+c_j^2)x_i^2+2(a_jb_j+c_jd_j)x_iy_i+(b_j^2+d_j^2)y_i^2}\ge \kappa |v_i|\\
&\sin\angle(A_jv_1,A_jv_2)=\left|\frac{(a_jd_j-b_jc_j)(y_2x_1-y_1x_2)}{|A_jv_1||A_jv_2|}\right|\le \kappa^{-2}\sin\angle(v_1,v_2).
\end{split}
 \end{align}
Let $Proj^+:=\left\{\mathrm{span}\{v\}|\ v\in \mathbb R^{2+}\right\}$ which is a compact subset of the projective space $\mathbb P^2$.  It is not hard to see that the second inequality of (\ref{E:Expan&Contrac}) yields that for any $\hat a\in \mathcal S_k$ and $n\in\mathbb N$ the map $\phi(\cdot,\hat a)$ induces a  contraction map on $Proj^+$ with a uniform contracting rate. By the contracting mapping theorem, we have that there is a unique $1$-dimensional space $E_{\hat a}$ such that
$$E_{\hat a}\in \bigcap_{n\ge 0}\bar\phi^n(Proj^+,\sigma^{-n}\hat a),$$
where we denote $\bar \phi(\cdot,\hat a)$ the induced map on $\mathbb P^2$ by  $\phi(\cdot,\hat a)$. By the uniqueness, we have that
$$\phi(E_{\hat a},\hat a)=E_{\sigma\hat a}.$$
The first inequality of (\ref{E:Expan&Contrac}) yields that $\phi(|_{E_{\hat a}},\hat a)$ is expanding with rate at least $\kappa$. The continuity of $E_{\hat a}$ on $\hat a$ simply follows from the second inequality of (\ref{E:Expan&Contrac}).\\

By applying exactly the  same argument, we can obtain that for any $\hat a\in \mathcal S_k$ there exists a unique $1$-dimensional space $F_{\hat a}\notin Proj^+$ such that $F_{\hat a}$ varies continuously on $\hat a$ and the following holds
$$\phi(F_{\hat a},\hat a)=F_{\sigma\hat a}\text{ and }\phi^{-1}(|_{F_{\hat a}},\hat a) \text {is expanding with rate at least }\kappa.$$
Note that $\phi$ itself is linear on $\mathbb T^2$, therefore the linearization of $\hat \phi^n$, $D_{\mathbb T^2}\hat \phi^n$, can be identified by $\phi$. Hence, $\hat \phi$ is an S2)-type system with continuous co-invariant splitting $\mathbb R^2=E_{\hat a}\oplus F_{\hat a}$ for $\hat a\in\mathcal S_k$.

title: Proof
body_md:
This theorem follows from Part A. of Theorem \ref{T:TheoryAnosovMix2} and  the following lemma:
 \begin{lem}\label{L:S1EntropyEquality}                    
 Let $\phi$ be an S1) system. Then the following holds
 $$\underline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)=\overline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)=h_{top}(\phi),$$
 where $h_{top}(\phi)$ is the topological entropy of $\phi$.
 \end{lem}

 \begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma \ref{L:S1EntropyEquality}]
It is straightforward to observe that $\overline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)\le h_{top}(\phi)$ by the definition. For the sake of simplicity, we will prove this lemma in the case of $h_{top}(\phi)<\infty$ only, as for the other case the  same argument is still applicable.
By the Theorem 17 in \cite{Bow3}, we have  that
$$h_{top}(\phi)\le \overline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)+h_{top}(\theta).$$
Since $\theta$ is equicontinuous, we have $h_{top}(\theta)=0$, thus
$$h_{top}(\phi)= \overline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega).$$
Therefore, it remains to show that $\underline h(M\times \Omega|\Omega)=\overline h(M\times \Omega|\Omega)$. It is sufficient to prove the following
\begin{equation}\label{E:FibEntrEqu}             
h_{top}(\phi|_{M_{\omega_1}})=h_{top}(\phi|_{M_{\omega_2}}),\ \forall \omega_1,\omega_1\in\Omega.
\end{equation}
Recall that
$$h_{top}(\phi|_{M_\omega})=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log N(\omega,\epsilon,n),$$
where
$$N(\omega,\epsilon,n):=\max\  \left\{card(E)\big|\ E\subset M_{\omega} \text{ is an }\epsilon\text{ separated set with respect to }d^{\phi}_{M\times \Omega,n}\right\},$$
and $d^\phi_{M\times \Omega,n}$ is the Bowen metric. For a given small positive number $\gamma>0$ and $\omega_1\in\Omega$, there exists $\epsilon_0>0$ such that for any $\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_0)$ and  $N_0\in\mathbb N$, there is an $n\ge N_0$ so that the following holds
\begin{equation}\label{E:NumSepaSet}             
N(\omega_1,3\epsilon,n)\ge e^{n( h_{top}(\phi|_{M_{\omega_1}})-\frac12\gamma)}.
\end{equation}
Without loss of generality, we assume that $\epsilon<\frac12\beta_0$ and fix such an $\epsilon$, where $\beta_0$ is as in Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing}. Letting $\beta=\frac12\epsilon$ and applying Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing}, there exists $\alpha>0$ corresponding to $\beta$ as in Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing}. Again, for the sake  of convenience, we assume that $\alpha<\beta$. By the uniform continuity of $\phi$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that for any $\omega',\omega''\in\Omega$ with $d_\Omega(\omega',\omega'')<\delta$ and any $x\in M$ the following holds
\begin{equation}\label{E:VarEst}         
d_M(\pi_M\phi(x,\omega'),\pi_M\phi(x,\omega''))<\alpha.
\end{equation}
We note that this $\delta$ depends only on $\alpha$.

Let $E_{\omega_1}\subset M_{\omega_1}$ be an $3\epsilon$-separated set with respect to $d^{\phi}_{M\times \Omega,n}$ satisfying $card(E_{\omega_1})=N(\omega_1,3\epsilon,n)$. For $(x_j,\omega_1)\in E_{\omega_1}(=\{(x_j,\omega_1)\}_{1\le j\le N(\omega_1,3\epsilon,n)})$ and $\omega\in B_\Omega(\omega_1,\delta)$, define a pseudo orbit $\{(y_i'(x_j,\omega),\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ by letting
\begin{equation}\label{E:PsOrbSepa}            
y_i'(x_j,\omega)=\begin{cases}
\pi_M(\phi^i(x_j,\omega_1)), &\text{ when }i\ge 0\\
\pi_M(\phi^i(x_j,\omega)), &\text{ when }i< 0
\end{cases}.
\end{equation}
By the choice of $\delta$ and  (\ref{E:VarEst}), it is not hard to see that $\{(y_i'(x_j,\omega),\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ is an $(\omega,\alpha)$-pseudo orbit. Thus, by Lemma \ref{L:Shadowing}, there exists a true orbit, denoted by $\{\phi^i(y_j,\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$, which is $(\omega,\beta)$-shadowing $\{(y_i'(x_j,\omega),\omega)\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$. Since $E_{\omega_1}$ is a $3\epsilon$-separated set with respect to $d^{\phi}_{M\times \Omega,n}$ and $\beta=\frac12\epsilon$, we have that $\{(y_j,\omega)\}_{1\le j\le N(\omega_1,3\epsilon,n)}\subset M_\omega$ is a $2\epsilon$-separated set with respect to $d^{\phi}_{M\times \Omega,n}$.

Also note that, $(\Omega,\theta)$ is uniquely ergodic, thus there is an $N_1\in\mathbb N$ depending on $B_\Omega(\omega_1,\delta)$ only, which satisfies that for any $\omega\in\Omega$ there exists a positive integer $m(\omega)\le N_1$ such that $\theta^{m(\omega)}(\omega)\in B_\Omega(\omega_1,\delta)$. This implies that for any $\omega\in\Omega$, the following holds
$$N(\omega,2\epsilon,n+N_1)\ge card (\phi^{-m(\omega)}E_{\omega_1})=N(\omega_1,3\epsilon,n)\ge e^{n( h_{top}\left(\phi|_{M_{\omega_1}})-\frac12\gamma\right)}.$$
Therefore, we have that
\begin{align*}
h_{top}(\phi|_{M_\omega})&=\lim_{\epsilon'\to 0^+}\limsup_{m\to\infty}\frac1m\log N(\omega,\epsilon',m)\\
&\ge \frac1{n+N_1}\log N(\omega,2\epsilon,n+N_1)\\
&= \frac n{n+N_1}\left( h_{top}(\phi|_{M_{\omega_1}})-\frac12\gamma\right).
\end{align*}
Since  such $n$ can be arbitrarily large and $\gamma$ can be arbitrarily small, we have that
$$ h_{top}(\phi|_{M_\omega})\ge h_{top}(\phi|_{M_{\omega_1}}).$$
Also note that $\omega_1$ is arbitrarily chosen, thus the proof of (\ref{E:FibEntrEqu}) is complete.
 \end{proof}
 To end the proof, it suffices to note that
 $$h_{top}(M\times\Omega|\mathbb P)=\overline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)=\underline h(M\times\Omega|\Omega)=h_{top}(\phi)$$
 and
 $$\underline d_{L^\infty(\Omega, M)}\le \underline d_{L^\infty_\mathbb P(\Omega)}.$$

body_md:
\label{R:SRBMeasure}             
Under the setting of this paper, S1) and S2) systems satisfy the conditions of Theorem \ref{T:SRBMeasure}, thus, roughly speaking, we have both existence and uniqueness of SRB measure for a given $\theta$-invariant ergodic probability measure $\mathbb P$.

For S1) systems, since the driven system $(\Omega,\theta)$ is uniquely ergodic, each S1) system has a unique SRB measure $\mu$. By the variational principle, we have that $$h_\mu(\phi)\le h_{top}(\phi).$$
Therefore, by Theorem \ref{T:SPHorseshoe}, there exist strong random horseshoes on marginal $\mathbb P$ whose entropy can approach  $h_\mu(\phi)$.

For S2) systems, for any $\theta$-ergodic measure $\mathbb P$, there exists a unique SRB measure $\mu$ whose marginal is $\mathbb P$. By the variational principle, we have that
$$h_{\phi}(\mu|\mathbb P)\le  h_{top}(M\times\Omega|\ \mathbb P), $$
$h_\phi(\mu|\mathbb P)$ is called the relative entropy of $\mu$ with respect to $\mathbb P$.
Therefore, by Theorem \ref{T:PHorseshoe}, there exist  random horseshoes on marginal $\mathbb P$ whose entropy can approach $h_\phi(\mu|\mathbb P)$.

label: D:RandomSet
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D:RandomSet}            
A map $X:\Omega\to\mathcal F$ is called a {\em random closed set} if, for every compact set $K\subset \mathbb E$, $$\{\omega\in\Omega|X(\omega)\cap K\neq \emptyset\}\in \mathcal B.$$

A map $Y:\Omega\to\mathcal G$ is called a {\em random open set} if its complement $X=Y^c$ (by this, we mean $X(\omega)=E\setminus Y(\omega)$ for $\mathbb P$-a.e. $\omega\in\Omega$) is a random closed set. Since $\{\omega\in\Omega|Y^c(\omega)\cap F=\emptyset\}=\{\omega\in\Omega|F\subset Y(\omega)\}$, $Y$ is random open set if and only if $\{\omega\in\Omega|F\subset Y(\omega)\}$ is a measurable event for every $F\in \mathcal F$.

label: D:RTran
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D:RTran}        
 $F$ is called {\em random topological transitive} if for any random open sets $U,V$ with $U(\omega),V(\omega)\neq \emptyset$ for all $\omega\in\Omega$, there exists a random variable $n$ taking values in $\mathbb Z$ such that the intersection $F^{n(\omega)}(\theta^{-n(\omega)}\omega,U(\theta^{-n(\omega)}\omega))\cap V(\omega)$ is non-empty $\mathbb P$-a.s..

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:MixToTran}            
  $F$ is topological mixing on fibers (see Section \ref{S:Setting} for definition) implies that $F$ is random topological transitive.

label: E:Hitting
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $U$ and $V$ be random open sets with $U(\omega),V(\omega)\neq \emptyset$ for $\mathbb P$-a.e. $\omega\in\Omega$. Let $\{x_i\}_{ i\in\mathbb N}$ be a countable dense set of $\mathbb E$. For $i,j\in\mathbb N$, define
$$\Omega^U_{i,j}=\left\{\omega|\ \overline{B\left(x_i,\frac1j\right)}\subset U(\omega)\right\}\text{ and }\Omega^V_{i,j}=\left\{\omega|\ \overline{B\left(x_i,\frac1j\right)}\subset V(\omega)\right\}.$$
It is not hard to see that each $\Omega^U_{i,j}$ or $\Omega^V_{i,j}$ is measurable, and $\mathbb P(\cup_{i,j}\Omega^U_{i,j})=\mathbb P(\cup_{i,j}\Omega^V_{i,j})=1$. Without loss of generality, we suppose that $\mathbb P(\Omega^U_{i_0,j_0})>0$ for some $i_0,j_0\in\mathbb N$. Since $F$ is topological mixing on fibers, for any $i,j\in \mathbb N$, there exists $N_{i,j}\in\mathbb N$ such that for any $k>N_{i,j}$
\begin{equation}\label{E:Hitting}          
F^k\left(B\left(x_{i_0},\frac1{j_0}\right)\times \{\theta^{-k}\omega\}\right)\cap B\left(x_i,\frac1j\right)\times\{\omega\} \neq \emptyset,\ \forall \omega\in\Omega.
\end{equation}
By the ergodicity of $\theta^{-1}$ and Poincare Recurrence Theorem, we have that for $\mathbb P$-a.s. $\omega\in\Omega$, $\{\theta^{-k}\omega\}_{k\in\mathbb N}$ will visit $\Omega^U_{i_0,j_0}$ infinitely many  times. Given $i,j\in\mathbb N$, for $\omega\in \Omega^V_{i,j}$, define that
$$n(\omega)=\min\{k|\ k>N_{i,j},\ \theta^{-k}\omega\in \Omega^U_{i_0,j_0}\}.$$
It is not hard to see that $n:\Omega_{i,j}^V\to\mathbb N$ is measurable and $n(\omega)<\infty$ for $\mathbb P$-a.s. $\omega$.  Additionally, (\ref{E:Hitting}) implies that for $\mathbb P$-a.s. $\omega\in \Omega^V_{i,j}$, the following holds
\begin{align}\begin{split}\label{E:TTran}        
&F\left(n(\omega),U(\omega)\times\left\{\theta^{-n(\omega)}\omega\right\}\right)\cap V(\omega)\times\{\omega\}\\
\supset&F\left(n(\omega),B\left(x_{i_0},\frac1{j_0}\right)\times\left\{\theta^{-n(\omega)}\omega\right\}\right)\cap B\left(x_i,\frac1j\right)\times\{\omega\}\\
\neq &\emptyset.
\end{split}
\end{align}
Although we only give the definition of the integer valued function $n$ on $\Omega_{i,j}^V$, it is not hard to extend $n$ onto $\Omega$ for which (\ref{E:TTran}) still holds for $\mathbb P$-a.e. $\omega\in\Omega$, since there are only countable many $\Omega^V_{i,j}$s.
Thus $F$ is random topological transitive.

label: D:RPO
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D:RPO}      
Let $\delta$ be a strictly positive random variable on $(\Omega,\mathcal B,\mathbb P)$. Then for any $\omega\in\Omega$ a sequence $\{y_n\}_{n\in \mathbb Z}$ in $\mathbb E$ is called an $(\omega,\delta)$ pseudo-orbit of $F$ if
$$d(y_{n+1},F(y_n,\theta^n\omega))\le \delta(\theta^{n+1}\omega)\quad\text{ for all }n\in \mathbb Z.$$
For a strictly positive random variable $\epsilon$ and any $\omega\in \Omega$ a point $x\in\mathbb E$ is said to $(\omega,\epsilon)$-shadow the $(\omega,\delta)$ pseudo-orbit $\{y_n\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ if
$$d(F^n(x,\omega),y_n)\le \epsilon(\theta^n\omega)\quad\text{ for all }n\in\mathbb Z.$$

label: L:RShL
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:RShL}       
Let the random hyperbolic set $\Lambda$ have local product structure. Then for every tempered random variable $\epsilon>0$ there exists a tempered random variable $\beta>0$ such that $\mathbb P$-a.s. every $(\omega,\beta)$ pseudo-orbit $\{y_n\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ with $y_n\in \Lambda(\theta^n\omega)$ can be $(\omega,\epsilon)$-shadowed by a point $x\in \Lambda(\omega)$. If $2\epsilon$ is chosen as an expansivity characteristic, then the shadowing point $x$ is unique. Moreover, if the $y_n$ are chosen to be random variables such that for $\mathbb P$-almost all $\omega\in\Omega$ the sequence $\{y_n(\omega)\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ is an $(\omega,\beta)$ pseudo -orbit, then the starting point $x(\omega)$ of the corresponding $(\omega,\epsilon)$-shadowing orbit depends measurably on $\omega$.

label: D:RSD
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D:RSD}      
Let $k:\Omega\to\mathbb N^+$ be a random variable, $A$ a corresponding random transition matrix, and define for $\omega\in\Omega$
$$\Sigma_k(\omega):=\prod_{i=-\infty}^{\infty}\{1,\cdots,k(\theta^i\omega)\},$$
$$\Sigma_A(\omega):=\{\bar x=(x_i)\in \Sigma_k(\omega):A_{x_i,x_{i+1}}(\theta^i\omega)=1\text{ for all }i\in\mathbb Z\}.$$
Let $\sigma$ be the standard (left-) shift. The families $\{\sigma:\Sigma_k(\omega)\to \Sigma_k(\theta\omega)\}$ and $\{\sigma:\Sigma_A(\omega)\to \Sigma_A(\theta\omega)\}$ are called random $k$-shift and random subshift of finite type, respectively. Moreover, define $\Sigma_A:=\{(\bar x,\omega): \bar x\in \Sigma_A(\omega),\omega\in\Omega\}$, which is a measurable bundle over $\Omega$, and also denote the respective skew-product transformation on $\Sigma_A$ by $\sigma$.

body_md:
\label{T:BMST}       
Let $U,V$ be complete separable metric spaces and $E\subset U\times V$ be a Borel set. If, for each $u\in E$, the section $E_u$ is $\sigma$-compact there is a Borel selection, $S$, of $E$. Further $proj(E)$ is a Borel set and $\rho_S$ is a Borel measurable function defined on $proj(E)$.
